# Compounding Pressures and Scaling Limits {#sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales}

::: {.epigraph}
> "[F]eedback is a method of controlling a system by reinserting into it the results of its past performance. If these results are merely used as numerical data for the criticism of the system and its regulation, we have the simple feedback of the control engineers."
>
> — Norbert Wiener, *The Human Use of Human Beings*, revised edition [@Wiener1989HumanUse, p. 61]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Why has system and chip design become harder to carry through, and where might AI assistance be useful?*

**Core thesis:** *Compounding pressures across physical scaling, specialization, software co-evolution, and verification demand new abstractions, but assistance helps only when it targets the work that actually limits the next design decision.*
:::

For decades, architects rode the compounding dividends of Dennard scaling and Moore's Law, where shrinking transistors switched faster and packed more tightly while power density remained flat. Once that combined dividend ran out, subthreshold leakage stalled supply-voltage scaling, wire resistance limited signal propagation within a single clock cycle, and thermal budgets left substantial fractions of a die unpowered or throttled (the condition known as dark silicon). Although architects have turned to specialization by deploying dedicated matrix engines in GPUs and neural processing units to sustain throughput gains, specialization multiplies coupled, nonlinear trade-offs across the hardware–software stack until the space of viable alternatives outgrows the engineering capacity available to explore it.

This chapter traces that causal chain from subthreshold leakage and interconnect resistance-capacitance (RC) delay to dark silicon, accelerator offload overhead, and expanding verification costs. The raw size of a design space says little about the cost of evaluating candidates within it, and machine-assisted exploration delivers value only when it relieves the specific bottleneck delaying the next design decision (@fig-ch02-cover-map).

![**Compounding pressures shift the architectural bottleneck.** Fading automatic technology gains, coupled design obligations across hardware and software, and finite simulation and verification capacity converge to limit design velocity. AI assistance helps most when it targets the specific engineering work delaying the next supported decision.](images/ch02-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch02-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which fading technology gains, coupled design obligations, and finite checking capacity converge on the work limiting the next supported decision."}

These pressures fall unevenly across projects, so the limiting bottleneck keeps shifting. Simulation throughput restricts one study; software runtime maturity, missing physical collateral, or formal verification capacity constrains another. Once architects see where design effort concentrates, they can identify the work that actually limits each decision and judge whether learned methods or conventional automation would relieve it better. Assistance should be aimed at that work, since architectural complexity alone does not justify applying AI.

## The Redistribution of Architectural Design Effort

The moonshot in @sec-moonshot asks whether an AI-native design system can make exploring thousands of hardware–software alternatives practical, an ambition that begins with a concrete engineering tension. When an architect considers expanding an on-chip Level-2 (L2) cache to alleviate memory bandwidth pressure, a capacity-focused simulation may favor the larger cache because it reduces misses, whereas in silicon the additional static random-access memory (SRAM) bitcells consume die area, lengthen interconnects,[^fn-rc-delay-c02] and add leakage current. Because that leakage reduces the power available to compute cores within a passively cooled mobile device's thermal envelope, a simulated reduction in cache misses answers only a fraction of the architectural question.

[^fn-rc-delay-c02]: **Interconnect scaling and wire delay**: While transistor switching delays decrease as gate lengths shrink, wire delay scales unfavorably. As interconnect cross-sectional dimensions narrow at advanced process nodes, wire resistance ($R$) rises sharply while parasitic capacitance ($C$) plateaus due to fringing fields between densely packed lines. Consequently, distributed $RC$ wire delay across long global lines increasingly dominates cycle times, making large contiguous structures (such as wide cache arrays or cross-chip buses) physically impractical to access within a single clock cycle.

Software introduces a parallel degree of freedom: loop tiling can compress the working set enough to fit within smaller on-chip buffers, but introduces transfer coordination, direct memory access (DMA) descriptors, and loop-tail control overhead. Evaluating these trade-offs requires executable software schedules paired with characterized physical memory macros. The architect must formulate which joint hardware–software combinations to explore and identify which empirical metrics can decisively differentiate them.

Earlier abstraction shifts made design complexity manageable. Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions allowed engineers to specify circuit behavior without manually placing individual gates.[^fn-rtl-c02] Automated logic synthesis and place-and-route tools generated detailed gate-level implementations, while formal equivalence checking and static timing analysis verified functional fidelity and delay bounds. The historical transitions reviewed in @sec-moonshot demonstrated that abstractions succeed only when paired with trustworthy verification oracles. The difficulty today is that exploring cross-layer, specialized architectures forces exponentially more coupled decisions through these expensive tool flows.

[^fn-rtl-c02]: **RTL as an architectural contract**: Register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions specify exact cycle-by-cycle state transfers between synchronous registers. While RTL serves as the legal contract for logic synthesis, equivalence checking, and timing signoff, its rigid binding of pipeline stages and clock domains makes automated architectural exploration challenging: modifying a datapath's latency or decoupling an interface often requires restructuring the entire RTL description rather than tuning a high-level parameter.

A *design path* carries an architectural hypothesis through candidate construction, tool execution, and empirical comparison. In the cache example, a design path evaluates two capacities under a representative workload, inspecting latency, dynamic energy, and leakage metrics. This progression becomes a closed *design loop* when empirical feedback updates design state to guide the next exploration step: an unfavorable energy measurement directs the search toward a smaller capacity paired with a tiled software schedule. Executing a fixed parameter sweep yields passive observations; using those observations to steer subsequent experiments closes the loop.

Each additional experiment consumes implementation effort, electronic design automation (EDA) compute licenses, and expert review. Its inputs span timing constraints, power intent declarations, RTL source, and execution traces.[^fn-eda-constraints-c02] Depending on the project, the primary bottleneck may lie in constructing candidate artifacts, running slow physical signoff engines, or triaging verification failures. Diagnosing that bottleneck begins with understanding why physical scaling breakdown shattered traditional abstraction boundaries.

[^fn-eda-constraints-c02]: **EDA constraint formats**: Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) and Unified Power Format (UPF) describe timing requirements and power intent for EDA tools. Implementation and verification tools use those declarations to check the design under the specified conditions.

## Technology Scaling Breakdown and Specialization Pressures {#sec-fracturing-technology-dividend}

For roughly thirty years, processor performance advanced under classical Dennard scaling, where shrinking physical device dimensions reduced transistor area and gate delay while voltage scaling allowed more transistors to switch faster without increasing power density (@tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison) [@Moore1965Cramming; @DennardEtAl1974Scaling; @HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Today, device technology still supplies transistor density, but it no longer delivers proportional gains in frequency, single-thread performance, or energy efficiency. Extracting performance now requires choices that tightly bind microarchitecture, software mapping, and physical implementation together.

### The Collapse of Dennard Scaling and the Shift to Specialization

To see why specialization became more attractive, consider the balance in the original scaling model. Classical Dennard scaling assumed that shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ reduced transistor area by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance by $1/\kappa$, supply voltage by $1/\kappa$, and switching delay by $1/\kappa$. With switching activity held constant, $P_{\mathrm{dyn}} = \alpha C V_{dd}^{2} f$ then scaled by $(1/\kappa)(1/\kappa^2)(\kappa)=1/\kappa^2$ per transistor. This reduction exactly counteracted the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density and kept dynamic power density constant.

The post-Dennard column in @tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison uses one deliberately simplified assumption set to isolate what changes when voltage and frequency scaling stop: transistor area continues to shrink by $1/\kappa^2$, gate capacitance per transistor falls by $1/\kappa$, and transistor density rises by $\kappa^2$, while activity factor $\alpha$, supply voltage $V_{dd}$, and operating frequency $f$ remain fixed. The dynamic-power calculation excludes leakage and interconnect capacitance, which do not obey this ideal active-device model.

| Device Parameter | Classical Dennard Scaling ($\kappa > 1$) | Simplified Post-Dennard Case | Limiting Physical Constraint |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transistor Area ($W \times L$)** | $1/\kappa^2$ | $1/\kappa^2$ | Gate pitch scaling continues |
| **Supply Voltage ($V_{dd}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Leakage and switching-speed trade-off |
| **Gate Capacitance ($C_{\text{gate}}$)** | $1/\kappa$ | $1/\kappa$ *(idealized)* | Gate and interconnect capacitance scale differently |
| **Operating Frequency ($f$)** | $\kappa$ | $1$ *(held fixed)* | Thermal dissipation and leakage limit frequency gains |
| **Dynamic Power Density ($P_{\mathrm{dyn}} / A$)** | $1$ *(constant)* | $\kappa$ *(under stated assumptions)* | Dark silicon and thermal limits |
: **Classical Dennard scaling versus a simplified post-Dennard case.** Shrinking linear dimensions by a factor $\kappa > 1$ historically kept dynamic power density constant while increasing operating frequency. With voltage, frequency, and activity held fixed in the displayed post-Dennard case, dynamic power density rises by $\kappa$; leakage, interconnect, and nonideal geometric scaling make real product behavior implementation-dependent. {#tbl-dennard-scaling-comparison tbl-colwidths="[24,24,28,24]"}

Writing transistor density as $\rho$, the post-Dennard dynamic-power-density ratio follows directly from that assumption set:
$$
\frac{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}'/A'}{P_{\mathrm{dyn}}/A}
= \frac{\alpha'}{\alpha}
  \times \frac{C'}{C}
  \times \left(\frac{V_{dd}'}{V_{dd}}\right)^2
  \times \frac{f'}{f}
  \times \frac{\rho'}{\rho}
= 1 \times \frac{1}{\kappa} \times 1^2 \times 1 \times \kappa^2
= \kappa.
$$
Dynamic power per active transistor therefore falls by $1/\kappa$, but the $\kappa^2$ increase in transistor density raises dynamic power per unit area by $\kappa$. In physical silicon, static subthreshold leakage, interconnect RC parasitics, nonideal density scaling, and dynamic power management govern the realized power density.

The classical balance broke down in the mid-2000s as supply voltage became harder to reduce. Lower voltage slows switching unless threshold voltage also falls, but lowering the threshold increases off-state leakage.[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02] Device physics therefore constrains a trade-off that engineers must make among speed, active power, and leakage; it does not prescribe one operating voltage for every design. As voltage reductions slowed, architects could no longer count on density scaling alone to deliver the earlier combination of frequency and energy-efficiency gains [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach].

[^fn-subthreshold-slope-c02]: **Subthreshold swing and leakage**: In a conventional thermionic MOS transistor, drain current decreases exponentially as gate voltage falls below threshold. The subthreshold swing is $S = \ln(10) \cdot (k_B T / q) \cdot (1 + C_{\text{dep}} / C_{\text{ox}})$, with an ideal lower limit of approximately $60\ \text{mV/decade}$ at $300\ \text{K}$ under these device assumptions. A threshold reduction $\Delta V_{\text{th}}$ increases off-state current by approximately $10^{\Delta V_{\text{th}}/S}$ if the other parameters remain fixed. The realized swing and allowable leakage depend on the device and operating conditions; the trade-off restricts continued voltage scaling.

Fifty years of microprocessor scaling data from Karl Rupp's CPU sample (1971–2021), joined with a 2012–2026 frontier compiled from the published specifications of twenty-five accelerators including GPUs [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @JouppiEtAl2021TenLessons; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @AMD2025CDNA3; @NVIDIA2024B100; @NVIDIA2013K20XBoardSpec; @AMD2021CDNA2; @Myrhang2023AMDInstinctHPC; @Intel2023Gaudi2Datasheet; @Intel2024Gaudi3Whitepaper; @NVIDIA2024BlackwellDatasheet; @NVIDIA2025BlackwellUltraBlog; @NVIDIA2026RubinBlog; @Cerebras2019WSE; @Cerebras2021WSE2; @Cerebras2024WSE3], map this architectural evolution across three eras (@fig-microprocessor-trends). In the *device-scaling era* (1971–2005), single-thread performance, clock frequency, and transistor counts all climbed by orders of magnitude, though at different rates. Around the 2005 Dennard boundary, clock frequency stalled near $3\text{--}5\ \text{GHz}$ in this sample, and single-thread performance growth fell from about 52% per year (1986–2003) to about 23% per year, dropping to single digits by the late 2010s [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. This slowdown ushered in the *parallelism era* (2005–2016), where architects turned to multicore integration: sampled hardware thread counts reached 96 by 2016 and 128 by 2020, while the maximum reported CPU power in each four-year bucket rose from about $200\ \text{W}$ in the mid-2010s to about $290\ \text{W}$ by 2021, where the CPU series ends without establishing a power ceiling for later processors. A third inflection around 2016 marks the *specialization era*, as dedicated datapaths became an increasingly important use of growing transistor budgets.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked plot was deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->

Accelerator counts reach 336 billion transistors (4 trillion for wafer-scale parts), and power ratings reach $1{,}400\ \text{W}$. Ratings mix thermal design power, board-power limits, and total graphics power, not measured workload power. The CPU series establishes no later power ceiling. Accelerator sources and six dated design reports appear in the text; the hatched band is a hypothesis.](images/fig-microprocessor-trends){#fig-microprocessor-trends width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Log-scale chart with CPU sample maxima ending in 2021 and accelerator specification frontiers extending to 2026. CPU frequency growth slows after 2005, while transistor counts and accelerator power ratings increase. A hatched band after 2026 marks a hypothesized AI-native design era; a separate rail dates six AI-assisted design reports."}

These diverging curves in @fig-microprocessor-trends illustrate the structural end of automatic frequency scaling and the resulting pivot to specialized architectures [@Sutter2005FreeLunch]. When supply voltage scaling stalled around 2005, power constraints capped the fraction of transistors that could switch simultaneously at peak frequency, creating the *dark silicon* wall [@EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon].[^fn-dark-silicon-c02] In the parallelism era, duplicating cores extracted concurrency from parallel workloads, but serial bottlenecks and thermal limits bounded the return on general-purpose multicore expansion.

Specialization reallocates silicon budgets to dedicated datapaths. Packaged accelerator transistor budgets climb from 15.3 billion in the NVIDIA Tesla P100 (2016) to 208 billion in the dual-die Blackwell B200 (2024) and 336 billion in NVIDIA's Rubin GPU (2026), while Cerebras extends integration to 4 trillion transistors on a single wafer-scale die. Published accelerator power ratings rise from the P100's $300\ \text{W}$ thermal design power (TDP) to as much as $1{,}400\ \text{W}$ total graphics power in the Blackwell Ultra generation (2025). These specifications describe hardware budgets, not measured application efficiency. Regular matrix and tensor operations can amortize instruction handling across large arithmetic arrays, enabling throughput gains through parallelism and reuse rather than renewed exponential clock-frequency growth.

The hatched band at the right of @fig-microprocessor-trends asks what comes next. Each earlier era found a new lever when the previous one flattened: device scaling, then parallelism, then specialization. One candidate for the next lever is the design process itself, because the cost of producing and checking a specialized design now limits how many such designs a team can attempt. The evidence for that candidate is so far a set of dated events rather than a trend. Learned macro placement entered the floorplans of Google's production accelerators in 2021 [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], a domain-adapted language model was trained on internal design data in 2023 [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo], and in 2026 an autonomous agent synthesized a RISC-V CPU and an inference accelerator [@Verkor2026DesignConductor; @Verkor2026DesignConductor2], Google reported incorporating an AlphaEvolve-proposed circuit into next-generation Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) silicon [@DeepMind2026AlphaEvolveImpact], and OpenAI reported AI assistance across the design of its Jalapeño accelerator [@OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. None of these reports includes a matched conventional baseline for schedule or total cost, so the band records a hypothesis that later chapters develop and that later evidence must settle.

[^fn-dark-silicon-c02]: **Dark silicon**: Silicon that cannot all operate concurrently at full performance within the available power and thermal budget. Power gating, clock gating, and reduced operating rates are among the ways a design manages that limit.

### The Limits of In-Core Microarchitectural Scaling

General-purpose processors continue to improve through branch prediction, speculative execution, wider issue, and better memory hierarchies. These mechanisms can expose and exploit more instruction-level parallelism, but their benefits must pay for the structures needed to coordinate that work.

The issue window illustrates this coordination cost: while adding entries lets an out-of-order processor find ready instructions farther ahead and widening issue lets it execute more of them together, completing instructions must broadcast their result tags to waiting entries and selection logic must choose among the ready instructions. Because enlarging the window increases capacitive loads on those broadcasts while widening issue adds comparators and forwarding connections, wakeup latency scales with content-addressable memory (CAM) tag broadcast lines across waiting entries and selection latency is governed by arbiter priority trees across ready instructions (even though a quadratic connection count is not itself a quadratic delay law). The implementation analysis of @PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective shows why wakeup, selection, and bypass structures can limit the benefit of wider machines,[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02] while wire delay further constrains the physical distances over which that coordination can occur within a single clock cycle [@AgarwalEtAl2000ClockRateVersusIPC].

[^fn-palacharla-circuits-c02]: **Issue-window circuit limits**: In an out-of-order superscalar core with issue window capacity $W$ and issue width $I$, the wakeup logic broadcasts $I$ result tags across all $W$ waiting instructions every cycle, requiring $I \times W$ content-addressable memory (CAM) comparators whose wire loading scales with window size. Ready instructions then feed selection logic, which uses priority arbiter trees whose gate delay grows with $\log W$ and whose layout routing introduces heavy wire capacitance. In deep-submicron processes, the physical wire delay across these densely routed CAM and arbiter structures, combined with the $O(I^2)$ forwarding paths of the bypass network, raises the cycle-time cost of each further increase in issue width, which is why wide machines partition or cluster these structures [@PalacharlaEtAl1997ComplexityEffective].

Pipeline depth introduces a related trade-off, as Intel's 31-stage Prescott pipeline illustrates [@BoggsEtAl2004Pentium4NinetyNm]: dividing work across more stages can support a higher clock rate, but a branch misprediction discards more inflight work and takes longer to recover from, so clock frequency alone cannot show whether the processor completes a workload sooner or uses less energy. Moving to multiple cores shifts the comparison again because coherence, memory ordering, synchronization, and workload partitioning determine how much parallel hardware is actually useful, explaining the appeal of specialization without implying that general-purpose microarchitecture has stopped advancing.

### The Specialization Turn and Accelerator Scaling

Specialization offers another use for the transistor budget. Regular computations can execute on many arithmetic units with less instruction-control overhead, provided that the workload exposes enough parallelism and the memory system supplies the operands.

Between the Pascal P100 and Hopper H100 generations, peak half-precision floating-point (FP16) arithmetic throughput outpaced off-chip memory bandwidth by roughly an order of magnitude (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier a). With precision held fixed and excluding structured sparsity,[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02] this divergence reflects an architectural pivot. P100 relies on conventional vector units, whereas subsequent generations integrate dedicated matrix Tensor Cores. The comparison illustrates the combined effect of specialized datapath acceleration and successive process nodes rather than an automatic application speedup [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper].

[^fn-structured-sparsity-c02]: **Structured vs. unstructured sparsity**: Mathematical weight pruning sets near-zero parameters to zero, but arbitrary (unstructured) sparse matrices introduce irregular memory indexing and load imbalance that frequently degrade performance on parallel vector and matrix hardware. In contrast, hardware-supported structured sparsity (such as NVIDIA's 2:4 pattern introduced in the Ampere architecture) enforces that exactly two out of every four contiguous values in a matrix must be zero. This fixed structural constraint allows dedicated multiplexing hardware to compress storage by $2\times$ and double dense matrix math throughput without the runtime overhead of sparse graph traversal.

Because arithmetic capacity expanded far faster than High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) supply, feeding these datapaths demands dramatically higher data reuse. If we define a workload's *operational intensity* as the arithmetic operations executed per byte transferred across the memory boundary, dividing peak compute rate by memory bandwidth gives the off-chip balance point (@fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier b). Across these four generations, that balance point escalates tenfold from 29 to 295 FLOP/byte. A kernel operating below that threshold cannot reach peak compute throughput even with zero control stalls; it remains bandwidth-bound. A kernel operating above it provides enough reuse to clear the memory bottleneck, though it may still encounter pipeline dependencies, load imbalances, or tail latency.

![**Arithmetic scaling outpaces off-chip memory bandwidth.** (a) Growth relative to P100 in dense FP16 peak throughput, HBM bandwidth, and thermal design power (TDP) across four GPU generations (2016–2022). (b) The off-chip balance point escalates tenfold from 29 to 295 FLOP/byte, demanding steeper operational intensity to saturate peak arithmetic. Hardware specifications exclude structured sparsity [@FoleyDanskin2017Pascal; @NVIDIA2016P100Datasheet; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta; @ChoquetteEtAl2021Ampere; @Choquette2023Hopper; @NVIDIA2022H100Whitepaper].](images/fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier){#fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart for P100, V100, A100, and H100 GPUs. First panel shows dense FP16 peak throughput growing much faster than HBM bandwidth and TDP relative to P100. Second panel shows the off-chip balance point rising tenfold from 29 to 295 floating-point operations per byte transferred from HBM."}

Architects respond to this divergence between arithmetic throughput and memory supply in four ways. To keep matrix engines from idling while they wait for operands, they can restructure algorithms for temporal reuse, change the computation to higher-density formats, widen physical interfaces with advanced packaging, or allocate substantial die area to on-chip SRAM caches.

These responses carry different physical and software costs. Expanding on-chip SRAM reduces off-chip traffic at the expense of die area, whereas wider memory interfaces and advanced packaging supply more bandwidth by taking on greater implementation and power-delivery complexity. Although software tiling can improve operand reuse within either organization, the right balance depends on the workload's capacity, bandwidth, latency, and power demands, so memory remains central to the comparison without acting as the limiting resource for every workload.

### Domain Specialization Tightens Cross-Layer Stack Coupling

Memory and thermal bottlenecks blur traditional stack boundaries. A layered view separates software optimization, microarchitecture, and device technology so that each can be reasoned about on its own, but specialization binds these tiers through shared power, thermal, and area budgets (@fig-tao-vs-taos). Specialization does not create this coupling; it tightens dependencies that already existed. A software tiling choice sets on-chip memory capacity, that capacity sets die area and wire delay, and those physical limits in turn restrict which software schedules remain viable.

An early model must therefore retain the dependencies that can change the ordering of alternatives. A compute-only model may favor a larger arithmetic array even when its data supply makes the added units ineffective. Once that accelerator joins a larger system, communication and unaccelerated work introduce further reasons for a local improvement to disappoint. Those composition costs are the next part of the argument.

## Balancing Specialization and System Composition

When physical scaling no longer yields automatic performance and energy dividends, specialization becomes the primary architectural lever. Yet a specialized block delivers value only within the system that feeds its inputs and consumes its outputs: local speedup must compensate for host dispatch latency, data transfer overhead, and the unaccelerated serial work remaining on the host processor. Partitioning that system across discrete chiplets or a wafer-scale fabric shifts where and how these penalties are paid. The first architectural decision is therefore what computation to specialize and what fraction of the workload can use it.

![**Specialization makes cross-layer dependencies explicit.** (a) A classical layered view separates optimization, architecture, and technology into modular tiers. (b) The specialization-coupled view reveals how domain specialization binds software mapping, microarchitecture, and silicon fabrication across shared power, thermal, and area constraints.](images/fig-tao-vs-taos){#fig-tao-vs-taos width="80%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side stack diagrams. The first panel shows optimization, architecture, and technology stacked in a top-down hierarchy. The second panel introduces a specialization block coupled across all three tiers, bounded by a shared thermal, power, and area constraint perimeter."}

### Specialization Traps and Amdahl's Law

Specialization spans a continuous spectrum rather than a binary leap from a general-purpose CPU to a custom accelerator. Designers can integrate vector and matrix units into general-purpose cores, assign data-parallel workloads to GPUs, construct domain-specific accelerators with custom dataflows, or restrict execution to specific operations in fixed-function application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Moving along this spectrum trades the breadth of workloads and software paths the hardware can execute for potential gains in energy efficiency and throughput density.

Moving along this spectrum also changes what a comparison must measure. Optimization targets differ between an energy-constrained mobile system-on-chip (SoC) (optimizing milliwatts and joules per frame) and a warehouse-scale data center (optimizing total cost of ownership (TCO) and throughput per kilowatt). A specialized block can only be fairly judged against the specific target it was engineered for.

The potential upside is large. For the H.264 video encoder studied by @HameedEtAl2010Inefficiency, a fixed-function ASIC was roughly 500 times more energy efficient than the four-processor chip multiprocessor the authors started from. The authors captured most of this efficiency gain by eliminating instruction fetch, decoding, and redundant data movement, while simultaneously exploiting massive parallelism and fused operations. The result belongs to that workload, and it shows why deciding what to specialize, determining which flexibility to keep, and shaping the software interface have become central architectural challenges.

This drive for specialization has spawned a wide diversity of designs, a period the team behind Project Brainwave, Microsoft's deep-learning acceleration platform, described as one of rapid architectural diversification [@ChungEtAl2018Brainwave]. Publicly announced AI accelerators span seven orders of magnitude in peak power and six orders in peak performance across training and inference workloads (@fig-accelerator-landscape) [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS]. Ranging from subwatt embedded chips to multi-kilowatt data-center clusters, with energy-efficiency contours stretching from 100\ GOps/W to 100\ TOPS/W, these roughly 180 designs form a dense, heterogeneous cloud rather than clustering around a single operating point.

```{python}
#| label: fig-accelerator-landscape

#|   distinguish training from inference parts, and dashed diagonals trace constant energy-efficiency contours
#|   from $100\ \text{GOps/W}\text{ to }100\ \text{TOPS/W}$. The resulting design space forms a dense, heterogeneous cloud

Points span from subwatt embedded chips at the lower left to multi-kilowatt data-center systems at the upper right, roughly seven orders of magnitude in power and six in performance. Dashed diagonal lines mark constant energy efficiency from 100 giga-ops per watt to 100 tera-ops per watt. Chips are circles, cards squares, and systems triangles; training parts are filled and inference parts hollow."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style
from _python.labels import place_labels

apply_style()

# Data: MIT Lincoln Laboratory AI accelerator survey, 2025 edition
# [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS], one row per publicly announced accelerator with a
# stated peak performance and power. Values are dataset-transcribed.
# Accessed 2026-07-19. Source data: data/datasets/chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rows = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter1-accelerator-landscape.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for d in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        try:
            perf = float(d["peak_performance_ops_per_s"]) / 1e9
            power = float(d["power_w"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        rows.append({"label": d["label"], "perf": perf, "power": power,
                     "form": d["form_factor"], "iort": d["inference_or_training"]})

forms = {"Chip": COLORS["workload"], "Card": COLORS["methods"], "System": COLORS["evidence"]}
markers = {"Chip": "o", "Card": "s", "System": "^"}  # shape as well as hue
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.0))
xline = np.array([1e-3, 1e5])
for eff, lab in [(1e2, "100 GOPS/W"), (1e3, "1 TOPS/W"), (1e4, "10 TOPS/W"), (1e5, "100 TOPS/W")]:
    ax.plot(xline, eff * xline, ls=(0, (5, 4)), color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=1)
    x_pos = max(2.4e-3, 10.0 / eff)
    ax.text(x_pos, eff * x_pos * 1.3, lab, fontsize=4.6, color=COLORS["muted"],
            rotation=34, rotation_mode="anchor", va="bottom", ha="left", zorder=1)
for form, color in forms.items():
    for iort, filled in [("training", True), ("inference", False)]:
        pts = [d for d in rows if d["form"] == form and d["iort"] == iort]
        if not pts:
            continue
        xs = [d["power"] for d in pts]
        ys = [d["perf"] for d in pts]
        if filled:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolor=color, edgecolor=color, linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.9, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=14, marker=markers[form], facecolors="white", edgecolors=color, linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.95, zorder=3)
for txt, x, y in [("Very low power", 0.02, 3.0e3), ("Embedded / autonomous", 3.0, 1.2e1),
                  ("Data-center cards", 5e1, 2.5e6), ("Data-center systems", 1.5e4, 2.5e5)]:
    ax.text(x, y, txt, fontsize=5.2, fontstyle="italic", color=COLORS["muted"], ha="center", va="center", zorder=2)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(8e-4, 7e4)
ax.set_ylim(3, 1e8)
ax.set_xlabel("Peak power (W)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Peak performance (GOps/sec)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker=markers[f], ls="", markerfacecolor=c, markeredgecolor=c, markersize=5, label=f) for f, c in forms.items()]
handles += [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=COLORS["ink"], markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Training"),
            Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=COLORS["ink"], markersize=5, label="Inference")]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3, borderaxespad=0.4)
curated = ["Maxim", "GAP9", "Jetson1", "Perceive", "A100", "TPU4", "H100",
           "AMD-MI300X", "B200", "Gaudi3", "CS-2", "DGX-H100", "GroqNode", "Tachyum"]
by_label = {d["label"]: d for d in rows}
items = [(by_label[n]["power"], by_label[n]["perf"], n) for n in curated if n in by_label]
place_labels(ax, fig, items, fontsize=5.0, color=COLORS["ink"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.095, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
```

The spread in @fig-accelerator-landscape illustrates the diversity of deployment targets rather than establishing which design is best, because the plotted points mix numerical precisions, supported operations, and chip, card, and system boundaries. Where a subwatt sensor processor emphasizes local storage and low-precision arithmetic to avoid costly off-chip transfers, a data-center accelerator devotes orders of magnitude more power to compute arrays and memory bandwidth. Within either regime, a favorable position on a peak-performance plot cannot replace workload measurements when choosing vector lengths, scratchpad capacities, dataflows, and scheduling policies.

Operating points in this design space also conceal differences in how operands reach arithmetic units. Systolic arrays maximize local operand reuse through fixed register-to-register pipelines, while streaming multiprocessors rely on massive multithreading and deep cache hierarchies to tolerate memory latency. Because each organization imposes distinct constraints on compiler scheduling, memory access patterns, and runtime invocation overhead, peak throughput and power ratings alone cannot determine which machine best serves a given workload.

In a composed system, a domain-specific accelerator (DSA) may handle dense compute while a general-purpose core retains control flow and irregular tasks. The runtime must move data and synchronize execution between them. Before committing die area and power to the specialized block, architects therefore need to determine what fraction $f$ of the workload it accelerates and how much the crossing costs. Amdahl's law makes that first comparison explicit (@eq-amdahl-communication).

$$S_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{1}{(1-f) + \frac{f}{S_{\mathrm{accel}}} + t_{\mathrm{comm}}}$${#eq-amdahl-communication}

where $S_{\mathrm{accel}}$ is the execution speedup on the specialized block, and $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is the added transfer and synchronization time, normalized to baseline execution time. The expression assumes that this added cost does not overlap useful computation. Even unbounded local acceleration cannot exceed $1/(1-f)$ total speedup when communication is free [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. Adding communication lowers that bound. The same reasoning bounded design-schedule improvements in @sec-moonshot; here it helps decide whether a proposed accelerator deserves its system cost.

The interpretation also depends on whether the problem size is fixed. Gustafson's law considers increasing the parallel work as more processors become available, as a training study might do with a larger model or dataset [@Gustafson1988AmdahlLaw]. A fixed-work latency comparison asks a different question. When a mobile-XR workload has fixed per-frame work and a fixed deadline, dispatch and synchronization consume time that additional arithmetic cannot recover. The compiler, runtime, memory traffic, and residual host work must therefore accompany the accelerator in the comparison.

That judgment can be made quantitative. Amdahl's $t_{\mathrm{comm}}$ lumps every communication cost into one normalized term, whereas the LogCA model separates the terms an offload actually pays: latency, overhead, granularity, computational index, and acceleration [@AltafWood2017LogCA]. For a payload of $g$ work units, host cost $C_h$ cycles per work unit, fixed invocation overhead $o$ in cycles,[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02] local compute acceleration $A$, transferred data $d$ in bytes per work unit, link bandwidth $B$ in bytes per cycle, and overlapped transfer interval $T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)$ in cycles (or, equivalently, with time expressed in nanoseconds, work in FLOPs, and bandwidth in gigabytes per second):

[^fn-host-dispatch-overhead-c02]: **Mechanics of invocation overhead ($o$)**: Launching work on an off-chip accelerator can involve command-buffer preparation, driver calls, queue submission, and a memory-mapped hardware doorbell. Buffer registration and address mapping may be paid during setup or repeated, depending on the runtime. User-space queues and persistent execution can reduce the work paid per launch. The relevant overhead is the measured cost on the workload's actual invocation path; physical-link latency alone does not determine it.

$$
T_{\mathrm{host}}(g) = C_h g,
\qquad
T_{\mathrm{acc}}(g) = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \max\left(0,\frac{d g}{B} - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right).
$$

The ratio of the two is the delivered speedup (@eq-logca-speedup-bound):

$$
S(g) = \frac{C_h g}{o + C_h g/A + \max\left(0,\, d g/B - T_{\mathrm{overlap}}(g)\right)}.
$${#eq-logca-speedup-bound}

In the nonoverlapped regime ($T_{\mathrm{overlap}} = 0$), offloading achieves net acceleration ($S(g) > 1$) only when the payload exceeds the break-even granularity $g^*$, obtained by setting $S(g) = 1$:

$$
C_h g = o + \frac{C_h g}{A} + \frac{d g}{B}
\implies
g\left[C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}\right] = o
$$

which yields

$$
g^* = \frac{o}{C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right) - \frac{d}{B}}.
$${#eq-logca-breakeven-g}

For a positive invocation overhead and $A>1$, this break-even granularity exists only when the denominator is positive. If we take one work unit to be one arithmetic operation, then $d = 1/\mathrm{OI}$ in bytes per operation. This connects the transfer constraint to the operational-intensity reasoning of the Roofline model [@Williams2009Roofline]. When intensity falls to or below

$$
\mathrm{OI} \le \mathrm{OI}^* = \frac{1}{B \cdot C_h\left(1 - \frac{1}{A}\right)}
$$

the denominator of @eq-logca-breakeven-g becomes nonpositive. At the specified acceleration $A$, transfer takes at least as much time per operation as offloading saves, so no payload size produces a speedup. Increasing $A$ changes the threshold, but cannot eliminate the transfer cost. This distinction separates an invocation cost that a larger payload can amortize from a per-operation cost that it cannot.

Those two terms call for different architectural remedies: lowering invocation overhead $o$ shrinks the payload needed to amortize each launch, whereas relaxing the operational-intensity bound requires either wider link bandwidth $B$ or fewer transferred bytes per operation $d$, since enlarging the payload alone cannot help when data movement grows in proportion to work.

Applying @eq-logca-breakeven-g to a real system requires measuring its invocation path, achieved transfer rate, host execution cost, and accelerator execution time rather than reading a link specification in isolation, because driver, runtime, synchronization, and protocol behavior all shape the costs a workload actually pays. Sweeping end-to-end execution time across payload sizes tests whether the predicted crossover occurs and how much transfer overlap shifts it. Even after startup overhead is amortized, nonoverlapped transfers still cap asymptotic speedup below the local compute factor $A$, which serves only as an upper bound approached when communication costs vanish; estimating that gap requires modeling a plausible invocation path alongside the datapath itself.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The unamortized offload wall"}
**The trap.** A team treats the local matrix-multiply acceleration of a neural processing unit (NPU) as the expected system speedup without measuring dispatch and transfer costs.

**The mechanism.** Invoking the accelerator separately for small layers can leave too little useful work to amortize each launch. Transfer costs add to that penalty. The host baseline also matters: vectorized execution can reduce host time enough to erase a benefit measured against scalar code. Both $C_h$ and the relative acceleration $A$ must describe that optimized baseline.

**The lesson.** Measure the complete offload against optimized host execution. Layer fusion and kernel batching can increase payload size $g$ and reduce intermediate transfers; a lower-cost submission path can reduce $o$. If feasible changes still leave the offload below break-even, retaining host execution is the supported choice.
:::

While the physical interconnect and invocation path set the baseline transfer and startup costs, the compiler and runtime determine the payload size, data reuse, and communication overlap that the workload actually achieves. This division of responsibility exposes where the operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers reach their limits. A Layer 2 search that tunes array dimensions, buffer capacities, or loop-unroll factors inside a frozen container can alter local acceleration $A$ and, through improved reuse, shrink transferred data $d$, but it cannot modify the invocation path governing $o$ or the physical link governing $B$. At fixed data movement, raising $A$ alone cannot push the break-even threshold $\mathrm{OI}^*$ below $1/(B \cdot C_h)$, whereas reducing $d$ raises achieved operational intensity and may clear the threshold without touching an interface. Claiming that an architecture needs new interfaces therefore requires showing that feasible reuse and mapping choices inside the existing container cannot reach break-even.

Moving the interface is a different kind of change. Kernel fusion, user-space submission queues, persistent kernels, and custom instruction extensions each alter $o$, $d$, or the payload $g$, and conventional hardware–software co-design teams make exactly these changes today. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would be permitted to propose such interface changes alongside the hardware parameters, but whether it can do so better or more cheaply than a conventional team remains to be demonstrated. The offload bound will therefore return as a software question once the hardware's composition has been examined.

### Packaging and Chiplet Composition Risks

Specialized intellectual property (IP) blocks rarely ship in isolation, since teams integrate them into systems-on-chip (SoCs) or distribute functions across chiplets. Smaller dies can improve manufacturing yield under random-defect models, although packaging, assembly yield, test, and interconnect costs also matter [@Murphy1964CostSize; @FengMa2022ChipletActuary]. While reusing a chiplet across products can spread its development cost over more units and let different functions use different process nodes, these benefits depend on compatible interfaces and a workable physical implementation. Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standardizes die-to-die communication, including physical interfaces and protocol support [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec], but does not choose the partition or establish that a particular package meets its power and shoreline-bandwidth needs.[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]

[^fn-shoreline-bandwidth-c02]: **Shoreline bandwidth density**: The communication bandwidth available per unit of die edge, often expressed per millimeter. In a side-by-side chiplet arrangement, interface placement, connection pitch, and signaling rate constrain the bandwidth that can cross the available edge.

Composition also introduces blocks whose implementation the system architect cannot inspect fully: because Arm has supplied processor IP as fixed hard macros [@Arm2013CortexA15HardMacro] and Intel distributes encrypted RTL [@Intel2024EncryptedRTLIP], integration relies on documented behavior, supplied models, and checks at the accessible interfaces. Although an interface specification such as Arm's Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) defines handshake and transaction-ordering rules at the boundary [@Arm2020AXI], reset, clock-domain crossing, or coherence assumptions that fall outside that contract can still make two individually qualified blocks fail together. Shared network-on-chip (NoC) traffic adds another interaction, where adequate average bandwidth can coexist with contention that misses a deadline, while partitioning must also provide test access since finding a defective die before assembly avoids spending a package on it [@IEEE2020Std1838].[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]

[^fn-kgd-yield-c02]: **Known-good die (KGD) and package yield**: For $N$ independently yielding dies, with assembly yield defined conditional on good inputs, a simple model gives $Y_{\text{package}} = Y_{\text{assembly}} \cdot \prod_{i=1}^N Y_{\text{die}, i}$. Without preassembly screening, defects in any constituent die can consume an otherwise usable package. Known-good-die testing reduces that risk by screening chiplets before bonding. Test escapes, correlated defects, and assembly failures remain; screening does not guarantee a functional finished package.

Automated exploration has to account for these integration constraints, because missing rules waste evaluations on physically infeasible combinations while overly restrictive rules prune away viable ones. The Semiconductor Research Corporation's Microelectronics and Advanced Packaging Technologies (MAPT) roadmap highlights inconsistent supplier data formats, syntax, and semantics as a primary obstacle to cross-vendor automation [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. Rather than treating unverified compatibility as silent permission or blanket prohibition, an exploration study needs to encode the interface rules it can verify and flag the remaining assumptions that require integration testing or supplier clarification.

### Wafer-Scale Communication Trade-offs {#sec-wafer-scale-communication-tradeoffs}

Wafer-scale integration explores a different balance between local communication and physical scale. Cerebras reports a $46{,}225\ \text{mm}^2$ area for its Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), which distributes computation and SRAM across a single wafer-scale chip (@fig-cerebras-wse-scale). Keeping more computation and storage on the wafer can reduce transfers over board-level links, but power delivery, communication distance, and defect tolerance constrain how much of that hardware can be used [@ReutherEtAl2025LAICS; @PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU].

![**Wafer-scale integration expands the area available for local computation and storage.** Area-proportional squares compare the first-generation Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine's reported $46{,}225\text{ mm}^2$ with the NVIDIA V100's $815\text{ mm}^2$, a ratio of about 57 [@Cerebras2019WSE; @ChoquetteEtAl2018Volta]. The squares represent published areas, not mechanical outlines or a wafer-cutting layout. The WSE contains 1.2 trillion transistors, 400,000 cores, and 18\ GB of on-chip SRAM, with communication crossing reticle boundaries. Keeping computation and communication on-wafer reduces reliance on board-level links but requires specialized power delivery, cooling, and defect tolerance.](images/fig-cerebras-wse-scale){#fig-cerebras-wse-scale width="70%" fig-alt="Area comparison diagram in which two separate squares compare the published Cerebras WSE area of 46,225 square millimeters with the NVIDIA V100 die area of 815 square millimeters, a ratio of about 57. The shapes do not represent mechanical chip outlines."}

The WSE's internal SRAM bandwidth describes a different memory boundary from the HBM bandwidth in @fig-ch02-accelerator-scaling-frontier and should not be read as a directly interchangeable specification. Although bringing more memory onto the wafer changes which transfers remain local, the benefit depends on how the workload maps onto the distributed storage and compute. In a wafer-scale GPU case study, physical constraints reduced usable capacity from a nominal 100 GPU modules to 40 [@PalEtAl2019WaferscaleGPU], showing why available silicon area is not equivalent to usable compute once placement, routing around defects, and software scheduling determine the communication that the workload actually experiences. Across these packaging choices, the same question persists: can the software use the proposed organization well enough to justify its costs, and what executable software path is required to answer it?

## Workload Volatility and Software–Hardware Coupling

The offload analysis demonstrates that software cannot be decoupled from architectural evaluation, because an optimizing compiler can fuse operations into a payload large enough to clear break-even thresholds while runtime driver traps can introduce enough dispatch overhead to erase all hardware gains. Evaluating a candidate architecture therefore requires an executable path to compile, schedule, and drive the hardware, and that path continues to shift after silicon is fixed as software stacks mature and emerging workloads change which hardware features matter. Architects face two distinct challenges: making a specialized mechanism usable upon tapeout, and ensuring it remains useful as software evolves.

### Executable Software Paths

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The *executable software path* connects a programming model or front end to the compiler, libraries and kernels, runtime, driver or firmware, and relevant operating-system and deployment controls. Different systems need different combinations of these components, but what matters is that the workload reaches the hardware with its intended behavior and without losing the expected benefit to overhead or data movement, which a peak floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) specification alone cannot establish.

One way to organize that work is a *compiler narrow waist*: a shared intermediate representation (IR) through which multiple programming models and hardware targets pass. Common transformations can operate on the IR, while target-specific lowering maps operations onto a particular machine. Halide separates an algorithm from its execution schedule [@RaganKelleyEtAl2017HalideCACM]; Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) provides infrastructure for transformations across levels of abstraction [@LattnerEtAl2020MLIR].[^fn-mlir-c02] Such abstractions can share work across targets, but each target still needs suitable lowering, runtime support, and validation.

[^fn-mlir-c02]: **MLIR dialect ecosystem**: Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) avoids a monolithic intermediate representation by organizing transformations into modular, domain-specific *dialects*. High-level tensor operations (such as linear algebra in the `linalg` dialect) undergo progressive lowering through structured control flow (`scf`) and arithmetic dialects down to low-level hardware representations (`llvm` or vendor-specific GPU dialects like `nvvm`), enabling optimizations to execute at the level of abstraction where domain semantics are most readily preserved.

The software that exposes hardware capabilities has a substantial implementation footprint (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall). While CUTLASS's architecture-specific headers contain templates and inline virtual assembly (PTX) statements for using specialized instructions (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall a) [@NVIDIACUTLASS], Triton's selected source trees include a shared compiler, target-specific lowering, runtime interfaces, and vendored headers (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall b) [@TilletEtAl2019Triton], and production serving frameworks such as vLLM also contain native kernels (@fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall c) [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. The measured source trees have grown across the sampled releases, although their line counts combine shared, vendored, and target-specific files rather than isolating porting effort or engineering maintenance hours.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The readable stacked panels and caption were deferred several pages under top-only placement. -->
![**Software source trees document an expanding implementation footprint.** Newline counts measured at release tags show (a) CUTLASS architecture-specific headers reaching about 208,000 lines and inline `asm volatile` statements passing 3,000; (b) Triton's selected trees reaching about 280,000 lines, including vendored headers, examples, and tests; and (c) vLLM native kernels reaching about 120,000 lines [@NVIDIACUTLASS; @TilletEtAl2019Triton; @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention]. Directory reorganizations limit comparisons of subcategories; these counts do not measure maintenance cost.](images/fig-ch09-software-porting-wall){#fig-ch09-money-plot-software-porting-wall width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Three-panel bar chart of source lines at selected release tags. CUTLASS headers grow to about 690 thousand lines, including about 208 thousand architecture-specific lines, and inline assembly statements exceed 3,000. Triton's selected source trees total about 86 thousand lines at v1, fall at v2, and rise to about 280 thousand at v3.7; totals include vendored headers, examples, and tests. vLLM native kernel sources grow to about 120 thousand lines, with a directory reorganization at v0.27."}

For the architect, the important consequence is that a hardware feature can add software development and maintenance work. A new matrix instruction needs a mapping that uses its operand layout; an asynchronous transfer mechanism needs scheduling and synchronization that preserve correctness. A shared compiler can reduce duplication, while hand-tuned kernels may expose capabilities it does not yet support. Neither route removes the need to evaluate the resulting program.

An executable software path bridges high-level programmer intent and physical hardware execution by funneling representations through a compiler narrow waist (@fig-codegen-narrow-waist). Front-end abstract syntax trees (ASTs) lower into mid-level intermediate representations such as MLIR and LLVM IR, where target-independent loop transformations and memory optimizations occur. Lowering stages then map these operations onto target-specific machine instructions and accelerator dataflows under physical power and timing constraints. The resulting binaries and runtime drivers supply the artifacts needed to verify functional correctness, kernel performance, portability, and software maintenance overhead.

![**Executable target software paths connect developer intent to verification checks.** High-level domain-specific abstract syntax trees (Python, Triton domain-specific languages [DSLs]) lower through mid-level control-data flow graphs (CDFGs) in MLIR dialects and LLVM IR at the compiler narrow waist, where workload intent, architectural mechanisms such as CPU instruction set architecture (ISA) extensions and NPU dataflows, and silicon constraints converge. Lowered machine code and runtimes are subsequently evaluated against verification checks for correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability.](images/fig-codegen-narrow-waist){#fig-codegen-narrow-waist width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of an executable target software path showing programming models, compiler representations, libraries, runtimes, and generated code connecting hardware constraints to correctness, performance, portability, and maintainability checks."}

The break-even bound in @eq-logca-breakeven-g makes the stakes of that interface precise, because in the nonoverlapped model acceleration pays only when operation granularity $g$ exceeds $g^*$ and operational intensity stays above $\mathrm{OI}^*$. The compiler and runtime influence both: whereas fusing operations can create offload payloads large enough to amortize $o$, eliminating intermediate tensor allocations in off-chip memory shrinks the transferred data per work unit $d$, shifting the offload's position relative to the break-even boundary.

Loop scheduling and instruction selection also determine how effectively a lowered kernel uses the target's register file and avoids pipeline stalls. In scalable vector architectures such as RISC-V Vector (RVV), compilers choose the active vector length and register grouping ($LMUL$, the register group multiplier) to trade loop control overhead against register pressure. Setting $LMUL=8$ amortizes instruction issue by operating on wide register groups, handling up to $\text{VLMAX} = LMUL \cdot \text{VLEN} / SEW$ elements per iteration (where $\text{VLEN}$ is the architectural vector register length in bits and $SEW$ is the selected element width in bits), while grouping the 32 architectural vector registers into eight-register bundles leaves four register groups [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. Because a fused kernel whose live values exceed the available groups can spill to memory, increasing traffic and reducing operational intensity, smaller groupings such as $LMUL=1$ or $LMUL=2$ provide 32 or 16 groups that may avoid those spills at the expense of executing more loop iterations.

This trade-off exposes a tension that peak vector width cannot settle, since a larger register group processes more elements per instruction but can force extra memory traffic when too many values remain live. Evaluating such a choice requires executable code on the relevant hardware or model, with the intended numerics, memory ordering, and application binary interface (ABI) preserved. Whereas autotuners such as AutoTVM search compiler schedules on fixed hardware [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM], a joint hardware–software study also changes the machine those schedules target, so that each proposed pair needs a comparable evaluation before its apparent advantage can guide a hardware decision.

An executable path makes the comparison possible, but does not keep it representative indefinitely. Compiler and runtime improvements can change the value of an existing mechanism, and a new workload can change which mechanisms are useful. Those changes may arrive while the hardware is still being designed.

### Changing Software and Fixed Hardware {#sec-software-changes-faster-than-silicon}

Software and workloads can change during hardware development. An architectural comparison may therefore need revisiting before silicon ships even when the RTL is unchanged. A design optimized for one model or compiler may encounter different shapes, schedules, or data types in deployment.

Several parts of the target can shift during this interval, including key-value (KV) cache management,[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02] compiler scheduling, and serving batch size. Numerical formats introduce a further choice: supporting 8-bit floating-point (FP8), 4-bit integer (INT4), or block-scale formats changes the arithmetic and data paths needed in hardware.[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02] Software may adopt a new format after the design has fixed which operations it implements directly.

[^fn-kv-cache-fragmentation-c02]: **KV cache scaling and memory fragmentation**: In autoregressive Transformer generation, attention keys and values for previously generated tokens are cached in memory to avoid redundant recomputation. Because sequence lengths grow dynamically by one token at each generation step, allocators that reserve contiguous buffers for a worst-case sequence length (such as 8,192 or 128,000 tokens) cause internal and external fragmentation. @KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention measured that such systems left only 20% to 38% of the memory reserved for KV cache holding actual token state, wasting 60% to 80% of that KV-cache allocation. Their vLLM system introduces paged allocation (PagedAttention) to assign non-contiguous physical blocks dynamically as tokens are generated.

[^fn-block-scale-formats-c02]: **Block-scale formats**: Low-precision number formats amortize shared exponent or scale metadata across a block of elements rather than storing independent metadata for every element [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]. Committing to one in silicon fixes datapath choices even as formats and workloads continue to evolve, requiring careful judgment of whether the choice will remain useful over time.

Before fabrication, hardware and software teams can revise the design together, although late changes become increasingly expensive. After fabrication, software can still expose more of the hardware's capability or adapt it to different uses. It helps to separate an implementation improvement on the same task from a change in the task itself: a faster kernel may strengthen the case for the existing design, whereas a different model shape or accuracy target may require a new comparison, and neither conclusion follows merely from a version number changing.

The architectural question is whether an upstream software shift invalidates an existing hardware evaluation, which cannot be settled simply by noting that two software versions or workload traces differ. Because specialization trades general-purpose flexibility for efficiency and throughput, the architect must identify which algorithmic assumptions are stable enough to build into silicon and design tests that measure when a workload change exceeds the hardware's remaining margin. Those assumptions span the kernel family, data types and precision, memory behavior, programming interface, deployment quality-of-service targets, and operating conditions (@fig-domain-specificity-shapes); none of them needs to stay frozen so long as shifts remain within the flexibility built into the design.

![**Specialization depends on assumptions about the target workload.** The six groups identify changes that may affect the value of a specialized design. A change calls for checking the affected assumptions; it need not invalidate the design or require repeating every evaluation.](images/fig-domain-specificity-shapes){#fig-domain-specificity-shapes width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram in which six source-to-target conditions surround the specialization scope: kernel family, data and precision, memory behavior, program interface, deployment and quality of service, and operating change. A separate bar states that changes in any condition can increase the verification burden."}

When a workload shift crosses one of those boundaries, earlier efficiency conclusions can fail quickly. An expanded working set that overflows scratchpad capacity triggers costly unmodeled DRAM spill traffic, just as a smaller serving batch size can shrink the payload per invocation below the break-even threshold $g^*$. Even when operational intensity, data reuse, and numerical semantics remain unchanged, shifts in compiler scheduling, synchronization, or runtime overhead can still alter delivered performance, so tracking the assumptions behind a design decision tells the team which measurements an update requires.

AI workloads provide a bounded example where model scale and computational demands shift visibly. While convolutional inference with fixed shapes tends to be regular, dynamic behavior frequently emerges in autoregressive Transformer deployments due to growing key-value caches [@KwonEtAl2023PagedAttention], variable sequence lengths, sparse mixture-of-experts routing,[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02] or distinct prefill and decode phases [@AgrawalEtAl2024SarathiServe]. Model scale also moves quickly. Epoch AI reported a four- to fivefold annual growth in training compute for notable models through May 2024 [@SevillaRoldan2024ComputeGrowth]; this book's own least-squares fit to a frozen July 2026 snapshot of the same database yields about 4.4-fold per year (@fig-training-compute-growth) [@EpochAI2025AIModels]. These records combine reported compute with Epoch's estimates, whose confidence varies across models. While scaling compute does not automatically constitute workload drift, empirical performance gathered for one model scale or training regime does not transfer to another without re-evaluating memory traffic and software assumptions.

[^fn-mixture-of-experts-c02]: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: A sparsely gated model activates only a subset of its expert subnetworks for each input [@ShazeerEtAl2017MoE]. Because this input-dependent routing forces memory traffic to vary from token to token instead of following one fixed schedule, hardware must be designed to serve highly dynamic memory demands.

An unweighted fitted line marks roughly 4.4-fold growth per year. AlexNet, AlphaGo Zero, GPT-3, and GPT-4 are labeled; all records used in the fit are visible."

```{python}
import csv
import datetime
import math
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _year(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-training-compute.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    for row in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")):
        yr = _year(row["publication_date"])
        try:
            flop = float(row["training_compute_flop"])
        except ValueError:
            flop = None
        if yr and flop and flop > 0 and 2010 <= yr <= 2026.6:
            pts.append({"yr": yr, "flop": flop, "name": row["model"], "frontier": row["frontier"] == "1"})

years = np.array([p["yr"] for p in pts])
logf = np.array([math.log10(p["flop"]) for p in pts])
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, logf, 1)
growth = 10 ** slope

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 3.3))
other = [p for p in pts if not p["frontier"]]
front = [p for p in pts if p["frontier"]]
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in other], [p["flop"] for p in other], s=8, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=2, label="Notable models")
ax.scatter([p["yr"] for p in front], [p["flop"] for p in front], s=12, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["workload"], edgecolor=COLORS["workload_ink"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=3, label="Frontier models")
xline = np.array([2010, 2026.5])
ax.plot(xline, 10 ** (intercept + slope * xline), color=COLORS["constraints"], lw=1.5, zorder=4)
ax.text(2018.0, 10 ** (intercept + slope * 2018.8), f"×{growth:.1f} per year", fontsize=6.6,
        fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], rotation=29, rotation_mode="anchor",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))

by_name = {p["name"]: p for p in pts}
landmarks = {"AlexNet": ("AlexNet", 6, -12), "AlphaGo Zero": ("AlphaGo Zero", -8, 11),
             "GPT-3 175B (davinci)": ("GPT-3", -8, 11), "GPT-4 (Jun 2023)": ("GPT-4", 6, 10)}
for key, (label, dx, dy) in landmarks.items():
    p = by_name.get(key)
    if p:
        ax.annotate(label, (p["yr"], p["flop"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(dx, dy),
                    fontsize=5.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"],
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["muted"], lw=0.45))

ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(2010, 2026.7)
ax.set_ylim(5e13, 3e27)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("Reported or estimated training compute (FLOP)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022, 2025])
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_spine].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.14, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

Relating software change to hardware development requires more than a model's publication date, and public product announcements provide one visible timeline (@fig-silicon-cadence). Measured between first announcements, the selected Apple SoCs arrive `{python} f'{min(apple_gaps_mo):.1f}'`–`{python} f'{max(apple_gaps_mo):.1f}'` months apart, whereas the NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 arrive `{python} f'{min(nvidia_gaps_mo[:2]):.1f}'`–`{python} f'{max(nvidia_gaps_mo[:2]):.1f}'` months apart, even though NVIDIA first announced Rubin only `{python} f'{nvidia_gaps_mo[2]:.1f}'` months after B200, roughly two years before it planned to ship. Because these markers locate products in time without revealing internal design durations or the dates when their architecture decisions became fixed, announcement intervals should not be read as design-cycle measurements.
