Internal development overlaps across generations, and a public announcement does not reveal when a particular architecture choice became expensive to change. Exposure to workload change must therefore be assessed for the design decision itself, using its expected lifetime and remaining flexibility.

Benchmarks are how computer architecture holds changing workloads stable long enough to compare them, and they also show what that stability costs. Within one MLPerf version, division, scenario, and accuracy target, the run rules allow architects to compare results from different systems while leaving submitters free to optimize their own software [@ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. That comparability is maintained rather than inherent to the workloads, and it lasts only as long as the community continues maintaining the tasks and rules.[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02] When those rules change, an earlier comparison may no longer answer the same question.

[^fn-metrology-calibration-c02]: **Metrological traceability**: A measurement result is traceable when it can be related to a reference through a documented, unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing uncertainty [@NIST2021MetrologicalTraceability]. While architecture benchmarks do not create this kind of formal calibration chain, explicit versions for tasks, run rules, and measurement procedures remain essential so that reviewers can verify when two results remain genuinely comparable.

For a target such as mobile extended reality (XR), the application name is still too broad to specify an evaluation. Sensor processing, tracking, and neural rendering can have different deadlines and data-movement patterns. Lighthouse supplies a 3\ W target, but selecting an XRBench workload [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] still requires choices about traces, model versions, input distributions, and quality targets. Those choices complete a particular study; they should not be inferred from the name *XR*.

A useful comparison records these inputs and identifies changes that would require it to be repeated. Workload changes can also expose interactions beyond the original hardware boundary. If a faster kernel increases pressure on shared memory or communication, the architect may need to enlarge the study to understand the system benefit.

## Expansion of System Boundaries Across Compute Scales

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The system boundary determines which interactions an architectural comparison can reveal. Suppose one accelerator finishes a kernel sooner but sends more intermediate data over a shared network. A device-level comparison may favor it, while a service-level comparison finds that congestion delays the complete request. The relevant boundary has expanded because communication can change the ordering of the candidates. Architectural dependencies propagate across five compute scales, from individual execution cores to warehouse-scale data centers (@fig-architecture-levers).

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The tall print-size scale diagram needs a full-page float option near its discussion. -->
![**The study boundary must include interactions that can change the decision.** Five scales illustrate architectural dependencies from core execution to warehouse-scale deployment. A broader study may reuse component models; it need not reproduce every lower-level detail at the same fidelity.](images/fig-architecture-levers){#fig-architecture-levers width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram of five architecture scales running from core through accelerator, system-on-chip or chiplet, wafer-scale system, and warehouse-scale system. Each scale adds named obligations to a common comparison path, which carries constraints, interfaces, workload and software paths, tool feedback, failures, and rejected alternatives into one cross-scale architecture comparison."}

At warehouse scale, aggregate demand and availability requirements make resource placement and sharing architectural choices. The relevant system can include servers, networks, distributed software, shared cooling, and facility power limits [@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Within and between nodes, interconnects such as Compute Express Link (CXL) introduce further choices about device and memory sharing.[^fn-cxl-c02] These mechanisms matter when they affect the objective under study, such as request latency, throughput, or cost of ownership.

[^fn-cxl-c02]: **Compute Express Link (CXL)**: A cache-coherent interconnect standard for processors, accelerators, and memory devices. Its memory semantics and switching support allow architects to treat device-attached or pooled memory as a system-level provisioning decision [@CXLConsortium2026CXL].

Because evaluating all of these interactions at cycle-level detail is computationally intractable, architects instead combine characterized component models with trace-driven or discrete-event simulators, testbed deployments, and production telemetry. What these combinations must keep are the effects that can change the design choice: since uncoordinated trace replays miss network queueing and average response metrics obscure the straggler latency that dominates tail-at-scale performance [@DeanBarroso2013TailAtScale], a wider system boundary calls for multi-fidelity models rather than brute-force simulation.

A governing design principle is to choose the minimal system boundary that captures every effect capable of altering the architectural decision. For local circuit timing, an isolated module boundary suffices; for end-to-end service latency, shared interconnects and pooled memory must enter the model. Even with disciplined scoping, the combinatorial explosion of hardware and software options quickly outstrips evaluation budgets, raising the core operational question: how much of the resulting candidate space can a team afford to evaluate?

## Combinatorial Expansion of the Architecture Design Space {#sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search}

Once the study boundary is set, hardware parameters, software schedules, and compatibility constraints define the space of alternatives to examine within it. The raw size of that space matters only in relation to the cost of constructing and evaluating each candidate, because a vast space with fast, informative feedback poses a very different engineering problem from a small space whose members each require days of implementation work.

Rather than treating candidate count as a direct measure of difficulty, a practical study rejects physically illegal combinations early, screens the survivors with fast analytical estimates, and reserves detailed simulation and physical signoff for promising finalists. Pricing evaluation across these stages reveals whether progress is limited by generating candidates, screening them, or qualifying the survivors, as published mapping, accelerator, and compiler studies illustrate.

The four tasks anchored in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors span the range that scale takes across hardware and software design. Candidate space volume does not measure evaluation work or decision confidence, because validity constraints and simulation fidelity differ radically between mapping, accelerator design-space exploration (DSE), floorplanning, and compiler tuning.

Timeloop [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop], an analytical framework for mapping and evaluating deep neural network (DNN) accelerators, illustrates a concrete lower bound on this combinatorial growth. For a convolutional neural network (CNN) layer with seven nested loops (batch size, input channels, output channels, output height, output width, kernel height, and kernel width) and a four-level memory hierarchy, loop ordering and level-bypass choices alone produce $(7!)^4 \times (2^4)^3$ arrangements, because the first factor provides a different ordering of the seven loops at each of the four memory levels while the second yields a binary bypass choice at those four levels for each of three tensor data spaces (inputs, weights, and outputs). Factorization choices enlarge this mapspace even further, although this formula represents neither the complete count nor a count of useful mappings, since it isolates two sources of growth before legality, capacity, and performance constraints eliminate most candidates.

| **Architecture task** | **Scale anchor** | **Why candidate count is not enough** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DNN accelerator mapping | Timeloop enumerates loop permutations, factorization choices, and level-bypass alternatives [@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. | Mapping is itself a combinatorial problem; architecture evaluation depends on the mapper and its constraints. |
| DNN accelerator DSE | MAESTRO, an analytical cost model for estimating DNN dataflow performance, reports 480M candidates, 2.5M valid designs, and 0.17M designs/s [@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO]. | Pruning rules determine which candidates are evaluated and which are never seen. |
| Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) block floorplanning | AlphaChip uses reinforcement learning to generate macro placements [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. | Reported gains depend on the cases, baselines, compute budgets, and downstream checks, which remain disputed in the reproduction, the reply, and the updated assessment [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement; @GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. |
| Tensor-program tuning | AutoTVM, a machine learning-based tensor program optimizer, describes tensor-operator search spaces on the order of billions of possible implementations for a single GPU operator [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. | Compiler schedules create a hardware-dependent search problem of their own. |
: **Large search spaces place different demands on evaluation.** Mapping, accelerator DSE, floorplanning, and tensor-program tuning combine candidate scale, validity constraints, feedback cost, and different evidence requirements. {#tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

\FloatBarrier

Candidate scale emerges from entirely different parts of the system. While Timeloop and MAESTRO demonstrate how quickly mapping and accelerator choices multiply, AutoTVM illustrates that software scheduling creates a vast search space even after hardware parameters are locked, whereas floorplanning exposes the complementary limitation that rapidly generating a macro layout does not guarantee routability or timing closure. MAESTRO makes this distinction especially clear: because at 0.17M designs per second we could score its full 480M-candidate space in under an hour, analytical feedback is plentiful and fast, leaving the hard decision of which apparent winners justify more expensive evaluation.

The three published search-space anchors in @fig-search-vs-eval-gap span roughly ten orders of magnitude. They represent different kinds of bounds: a reported accelerator exploration, an order-of-magnitude software estimate, and a mapping-space lower bound. Their spread shows how scale varies across design layers; it does not measure the difficulty of a single task.

Together, these examples separate the size of a search space from the resources needed to learn from it. The next question is what more detailed evaluation reveals, and why a team cannot simply apply every available check to every candidate.

## Evaluation Bottlenecks Across Physical Feasibility, Simulation, and Verification

Evaluation becomes expensive for three distinct reasons, and distinguishing them helps determine which additional work would make a comparison more useful:

1. **Physical implementation:** Timing, routing, power delivery, and thermal behavior can change whether a candidate is feasible or attractive.
2. **Simulation throughput:** Detailed timing models, hardware emulators, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) platforms require different investments in setup and execution.
3. **Functional verification:** Tests and proofs must address the relevant behaviors and properties, including interactions absent from performance workloads.

Any of these may limit a study. Physical constraints come first because they explain why a favorable high-level estimate may need revision before more evaluation is worthwhile.

### Physical Constraints {#sec-physical-constraints-move-into-architecture}

Physical effects create a tension between early comparison and implementation detail. A model simple enough to screen many candidates may omit a hotspot, supply-voltage drop, or routing constraint that changes the outcome. Detailed checks can expose these effects, but need more complete inputs and more tool time. The architect must decide which physical information is needed early and which uncertainties can wait until the candidate is developed further.

Power delivery and heat removal illustrate the problem on different time scales. When many units become active together, the changing current can cause a transient supply drop through the resistance and inductance of the delivery network.[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02] Whether that drop causes a timing failure depends on the operating point and available margin. Sustained activity creates a different question: can the package remove heat from the locations where it is generated? In a stacked design, the placement of active logic and the heat-removal path matter as well as total power. An average-power estimate alone answers neither question.

[^fn-di-dt-drop-c02]: **Inductive voltage transients ($L \frac{di}{dt}$)**: Power delivery networks contain parasitic inductance ($L$) distributed across printed circuit board planes, package balls, and micro-bumps. When an un-gated vector or matrix unit abruptly transitions from idle to full execution within one or two clock cycles, the rate of current change ($\frac{di}{dt}$) becomes large. The resulting induced voltage drop ($\Delta V = L \frac{di}{dt}$) compounds the steady-state resistive drop ($IR$), causing a transient voltage sag that can collapse the core supply rail below minimum operating voltage ($V_{\text{min}}$) and induce timing errors unless mitigated by on-die decoupling capacitors and conservative voltage guardbands.

The scaling discussion in @sec-fracturing-technology-dividend explains why a new process cannot be assumed to resolve these interactions. Because logic cells, SRAM macros, and interconnects have different scaling behavior and implementation constraints, returning to the opening cache example requires estimating the area, access time, energy, and leakage of the available memory macro together with its connections, rather than relying on a nominal process label.

Data movement provides a useful quantitative example. The 45\ nm reference values collected by @Horowitz2014Energy place a 32-bit integer addition near 0.1\ pJ, SRAM accesses in the displayed range at 10–100\ pJ, and off-chip DRAM accesses at 1.3–2.6\ nJ (@fig-data-movement-energy-scale), where the access widths and memory sizes differ as labeled in the figure. Because these historical values illustrate why a small reduction in arithmetic can be outweighed by additional memory traffic rather than supplying energy estimates for a current process, a system estimate must combine the relevant operation counts with costs characterized for its own implementation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-data-movement-energy-scale
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Data movement can dominate arithmetic energy.** Reference $45\ \text{nm}$ energy values from @Horowitz2014Energy
#|   demonstrate a disparity of more than four orders of magnitude between local arithmetic (0.1\ pJ for a 32-bit integer add)
#|   and memory access (10–100\ pJ for on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM), 1.3–2.6\ nJ for off-chip DRAM, a $13{,}000\text{--}26{,}000\times$
#|   energy penalty). Architectural comparisons must represent data locality, buffer hierarchies, and memory
#|   traffic rather than counting arithmetic operations in isolation. Transcribed order-of-magnitude anchors,
#|   not current-node device estimates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale plot comparing arithmetic and memory-access energy, showing a 32-bit integer add at 0.1 picojoules, static random-access memory (SRAM) accesses from 10 to 100 picojoules, and an off-chip DRAM access range from 1.3 to 2.6 nanojoules."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style, draw_range_rows, row_axis, top_log_axis

# Source dataset: data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm).
# Values are read from the CSV; ratios to the 32-bit integer add are computed here.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    src = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#"))]

baseline = float(src[0]["energy_low_pj"])


def _fmt_ratio(value):
    ratio = value / baseline
    return f"{ratio / 1000:.0f}k" if ratio >= 1000 and value >= 1000 else f"{ratio:.0f}"


rows = []
for r in src:
    low, high = float(r["energy_low_pj"]), float(r["energy_high_pj"])
    op, width = r["operation_or_access"], r["width_or_capacity"]
    if "SRAM" in op:
        capacity = width.replace(" 64 bit", "")
        label, note = f"{capacity} SRAM access", "64b access"
        color = COLORS["orange"] if high >= 100 else COLORS["green"]
    elif "DRAM" in op:
        label, note, color = "off-chip DRAM access", "64b access", COLORS["red"]
    else:
        label, note, color = f"{width.replace(' bit', 'b')} {op}", "local arithmetic", COLORS["blue"]
    right = f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}$\\times$" if low == high else f"{_fmt_ratio(low)}–{_fmt_ratio(high)}$\\times$"
    rows.append({"display_label": label, "display_note": note, "energy_low_pj": low,
                 "energy_high_pj": high, "right_label": right, "color": color})

apply_style()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 3.2))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.40, right=0.80, top=0.82, bottom=0.08)

row_axis(ax, len(rows))
top_log_axis(
    ax,
    xlim=(0.06, 4000),
    xticks=[0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000],
    xticklabels=["0.1 pJ", "1 pJ", "10 pJ", "100 pJ", "1 nJ"],
    xlabel="rough energy per operation or access",
)
draw_range_rows(ax, rows, low_key="energy_low_pj", high_key="energy_high_pj", label_x=-0.82, right_x=1.04, label_fontsize=6.6, note_fontsize=5.4, right_fontsize=6.1, label_dy=-0.17, note_dy=0.23)

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

To compare designs, we can group their energy costs by where the work occurs. The decomposition below separates computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage. Each term must be estimated for the workload and implementation being studied; the historical reference ratios do not supply those totals.
$$
E_{\mathrm{system}} = E_{\mathrm{compute}} + E_{\mathrm{memory}} + E_{\mathrm{interconnect}} + E_{\mathrm{control}} + E_{\mathrm{leakage}}
$${#eq-system-energy-decomposition}

The decomposition in @eq-system-energy-decomposition gives the memory hierarchy an explicit place in the comparison. The *memory wall* described by @WulfMcKee1995HittingMemoryWall concerns the growing importance of memory stalls as processors improve faster than memory latency. Its consequence depends on how often the workload reaches the slower level and how much latency can be hidden. The energy comparison similarly depends on traffic, rather than access cost alone.

Communication among cores and accelerator tiles adds another term. Offered traffic can exceed a network-on-chip link's capacity, causing queueing and backpressure even when the arithmetic units have spare capacity. The physical layout must also provide the wires needed by the chosen topology. Network traffic congestion and physical routing congestion are related implementation concerns, but they are not the same phenomenon.

The decomposition also exposes a possible proxy mismatch (@fig-waterbed-effect). A candidate can reduce compute energy while adding memory accesses and communication. If those added costs exceed the compute saving, total system energy rises and a compute-only metric ranks the candidates incorrectly. Establishing whether this reversal occurs requires the workload's traffic and the implementation costs of both candidates.

![**A compute saving must be compared with the other energy changes it causes.** This dependency diagram identifies the terms needed to compare a candidate with its baseline. The sign of the total energy change depends on the sum of the changes in computation, memory, interconnect, control, and leakage; a lower compute term alone does not determine it. Boxes and arrows encode dependencies, not measured magnitudes.](images/fig-waterbed-effect){#fig-waterbed-effect width="100%" fig-alt="Unscaled dependency diagram connecting a compute-energy reduction and changes in memory, interconnect, control, and leakage to the total system energy change."}

When evaluation omits data movement and wire parasitics, the missing energy terms can be large enough to invert candidate rankings (@fig-waterbed-effect). Although early analytical models can incorporate rough interconnect estimates, placement and routing determine the realized physical wire lengths, congestion, and parasitic capacitance [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign], so an automated search guided by an incomplete proxy score can promote configurations that fail physical implementation; checking selected candidates with a more detailed model helps reveal how often that bias occurs for a given proxy and design.

The same discipline applies to power analysis. Early activity and placement estimates, including learned predictors such as PowerNet's IR-drop model [@XieEtAl2020PowerNet] within the inputs and conditions they cover, can flag a dense mapping that deserves closer inspection even when average power is acceptable. Because electrical supply droops and steady-state heat removal act on different timescales, thermal analysis and power-delivery analysis must address their respective effects separately, and passing a thermal check cannot establish that a rapid current transient is harmless.

Vector execution illustrates this policy interaction concretely. Although adding 512-bit vector units to general-purpose CPU cores raises peak floating-point throughput, sustained AVX-512 execution on Intel's Skylake-generation server processors could trigger frequency-license offsets that lowered the clock for scalar work on the same core. Because the size of such effects varies by processor generation and peak vector width alone does not determine final application speed, architects must measure active-frequency policies alongside the exact mix of vector and nonvector work on the target processor.

During timing signoff, engineering teams evaluate multiple analysis views that pair operating modes with specific process corners using static timing signoff tools such as Cadence Tempus [@Cadence2021Tempus].[^fn-pvt-corners-c02] A design can clear one view while failing another. Because physical-design tools rely on heuristic optimization, a single failed closure attempt rarely indicates whether the candidate or a flawed tool setup caused the failure. Comparing constraints, seeds, and repeated outcomes separates true design flaws from tool artifacts.[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]

[^fn-pvt-corners-c02]: **Multi-mode multi-corner (MMMC) timing closure**: Physical signoff tools evaluate a circuit across specified operating modes and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions. Slow analysis views expose setup-time violations, while fast views expose hold-time violations where data arrives too early relative to the receiving clock. The relevant temperature and voltage combinations come from characterized libraries; their ordering cannot be inferred from temperature alone. Advanced processes also require appropriate treatment of device self-heating and statistical on-chip variation, while processes with backside power delivery add its electrical and thermal effects. A candidate that meets cycle limits at nominal conditions may still fail timing or reliability checks in another required view.

[^fn-eda-tool-noise-c02]: **EDA tool non-determinism and noise floors**: Physical synthesis, placement, and detailed routing rely on stochastic heuristics, including simulated annealing, force-directed relaxation, and multi-threaded maze routing. Minor variations in netlist declaration order or random seed initialization can shift worst negative slack (WNS) and total wirelength on identical RTL. The size of that spread depends on the tool, design, and flow, so it must be measured for the flow in use; @sec-incremental-churn-dispersion reports one such measurement across twenty placement seeds. In automated AI exploration loops, agents can easily mistake an artifact of tool noise for an architectural breakthrough, or discard a superior microarchitecture because the placer hit an unfavorable local minimum. Bounded multi-seed calibration is necessary to separate true architectural merit from tool noise.

Design-rule checks (DRCs) introduce further physical constraints. Routing must satisfy restricted design rules, including minimum wire and via spacing [@KahngEtAl2011VLSIPhysicalDesign]. Moving a single macro can spawn numerous violations, and repairing one can alter neighboring routes and expose fresh errors. If an automated flow cannot interpret these markers, it shifts a repetitive cleanup and rerouting burden onto implementation engineers.

An illustrative scenario shows where a Layer 2 optimizer can run into this friction. Suppose it sweeps macro floorplan coordinates $\theta$ inside a fixed die outline and scores each candidate with a fast wirelength estimate or learned surrogate. Such proxies can track average wirelength while missing local pin density, routing channel blockages, and multi-corner timing. If the favored placements crowd memory interfaces into dense clusters, the router may run short of tracks and return timing violations and design-rule markers that the proxy never predicted. Within the container, the optimizer cannot reshape pipeline registers, re-partition blocks, or change interface contracts, so the repair falls to implementation engineers unless the proxy is recalibrated or the search is allowed to move those boundaries. How often this happens depends on the design, the proxy, and the flow; the scenario identifies a failure to check for, not a measured rate.

Interpreting a later physical failure requires the exact design and assumptions that produced it. The retained RTL, parameters, constraints, and implementation outputs let an architect distinguish a design problem from a mismatched input. Electronic design automation (EDA) tools also consume representations beyond RTL, including Library Exchange Format / Design Exchange Format (LEF/DEF) and Liberty timing files.[^fn-lef-def-c02] The execution mechanics are developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; here the consequence is that preparing and preserving compatible inputs is part of evaluation work.

[^fn-lef-def-c02]: **LEF/DEF and Liberty**: In place-and-route flows, LEF carries the abstract physical information used to place and connect blocks, while DEF records design-specific physical information, such as placement and routing, even before those steps are complete [@Si2LEFDEF]. Meanwhile, Liberty provides characterized cell models covering timing, power, noise, and related behaviors [@Synopsys2012LibertyFormat]. Physical design relies on these implementation formats to expose details omitted from high-level architectural descriptions.

Multi-fidelity methods pair inexpensive models with selected evaluations that resolve their important omissions [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. The appropriate check depends on the question: gate-level functional simulation, static timing analysis, and thermal analysis provide different information. Using a more expensive tool helps only if it addresses the uncertainty that could change the decision.

While an inexpensive energy proxy supports early screening, finalists need an accurate power model before the team commits to a power or efficiency decision. A design can lead on advertised peak throughput yet degrade on real application workloads due to memory stalls and runtime overhead. One generation of AMD processors illustrates how wide that gap between an advertised specification and delivered work can open in practice.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A design that won on the spec sheet"}
**The claim.** In the Bulldozer generation (Zambezi, 2011), AMD grouped two integer cores behind a shared front end and floating-point unit while pushing clock frequency hard [@BurgessEtAl2011Bulldozer]. Core counts and frequencies are easy to advertise, so they made compelling marketing points. In sharing those structures, the design team traded per-thread capacity for aggregate throughput.
**The gap.** Those figures did not reflect how real workloads used the machine. The shared structures became bottlenecks when threads competed for them, and the higher frequencies raised power draw. The later FX-9590 part carried a 220\ W thermal design power [@AMDFXQuickReference].
**The lesson.** Because core count and clock rate alone cannot settle the comparison, shared structures must be evaluated with workloads that expose contention alongside power and frequency behavior, which explains why AMD's later Zen design placed renewed emphasis on per-core performance and efficiency [@AMDZen].
:::

### Simulation Throughput and Fidelity {#sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive}

Once a model includes the effects needed for a comparison, execution time becomes a constraint of its own. Longer workloads and more candidate configurations compete for compute, tool licenses, and the time needed to interpret results. The question is how much representative behavior the available evaluation budget can cover.

The 2013 zsim study described detailed gem5, Flexus, and MARSS configurations running at about two hundred thousand target instructions per host second [@ZSim]. That historical rate illustrates the cost of detailed modeling; present throughput depends on the simulator, configuration, workload, and host. A study must measure its own execution rate before multiplying workload lengths and candidate counts into an evaluation budget.

Architectural simulators, compiled RTL simulation, hardware emulators, and FPGA platforms trade setup effort against execution capacity while modeling different physical and behavioral details. Whereas a fast architectural simulator may simplify cycle-level timing interactions, Verilator executes an RTL model directly, and FireSim uses FPGA acceleration to run full-system, cycle-exact RTL simulations [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Even an RTL model omits routed wire delays and thermal behavior, so each tool's accuracy must be judged for the specific behavior it represents, and the useful choice is the one whose model and execution capacity answer the study's question at an acceptable total cost.

When full-workload execution is too slow, sampling can reduce execution cost without simply removing model detail: SimPoint selects representative program regions [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], while SMARTS uses statistical sampling with error estimates [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. Analytical screening, sampled detailed simulation, and full-workload execution can then complement one another, provided the study records which behavior the sample represents, how initialization and warmup are handled, and which conclusions require additional runs.

The allocation decision has two risks: a cheap estimate may discard a promising candidate or send an unsuitable one into an expensive evaluation. More representative simulation can reduce uncertainty about performance, but it does not establish correctness for every behavior the design permits. That remaining obligation leads to verification.

### Verification Bottlenecks

Adding a single state-holding flip-flop doubles the number of encoded states, meaning a design with $n$ sequential state elements can technically encode up to $2^n$ states. In practice, the reachable subset is far smaller because it depends on reset sequences and valid transition logic; verification flows therefore avoid blind enumeration of every encoded state.

For a large design, brute-force enumeration is generally impractical. Verification teams instead combine functional coverage targets, SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), formal checks, constrained-random and directed tests, regressions, and unresolved-defect reviews. Coverage describes the behaviors or requirements that the verification plan intended to exercise; a completed coverage target is not proof that every possible bug is absent. A new architectural organization can require new tests and properties even when much of the implementation is reused.

This is why verification effort belongs beside power, performance, and area (PPA) when architects compare candidates. A speculative cache-coherence protocol might show an impressive simulated throughput gain and still be the wrong choice if checking its transient states and race conditions exceeds the design-program budget.

Simulation and formal methods provide different kinds of assurance. Whereas simulation exercises selected behaviors under supplied stimuli, a completed formal proof establishes a stated property for all behaviors covered by the model and its assumptions, although the solver may not be able to complete that proof. Bounded model checking (BMC) searches behaviors up to a specified depth, where finding no counterexample within that bound is generally not an unbounded proof, while combinational equivalence checking asks whether two combinational descriptions compute the same Boolean function. These techniques can complement one another, provided that their scopes and assumptions remain explicit [@Clarke2018ModelChecking].

The semiconductor industry has grappled with this verification pressure for over a quarter of a century. As far back as 2001, the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) Design chapter declared verification "a bottleneck that has now reached crisis proportions" [@ITRS2001Design]. Today, the Semiconductor Research Corporation's MAPT roadmap explicitly warns of a widening verification gap looming across future technology transitions [@SemiconductorResearchCorporation2023MAPT]. This history is reason enough to check verification capacity whenever someone proposes generating architectural candidates faster, but it does not imply that verification will be the limiting constraint in every design program.

Staffing surveys give one view of how the verification share introduced in @sec-moonshot grew over time. In the 2022 Wilson Research Group study, demand for verification engineers on integrated circuit (IC) and ASIC projects grew at about 6.2% per year from 2007 to 2022, against about 2.7% per year for design engineers [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. Compounded over fifteen years, that is roughly two and a half times the 2007 verification staffing against one and a half times the design staffing (@fig-verification-demand-scissors). These are relative changes in surveyed staffing, not measurements of the time needed to verify an additional candidate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-verification-demand-scissors
```

The indexed lines in @fig-verification-demand-scissors show why verification capacity deserves explicit attention in a design plan. They do not identify the cause of the growth or determine the bottleneck in a particular project. The next comparison asks a different question: what do the surveys report about first-silicon outcomes alongside that effort?

Industry survey data place these results in perspective (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors). In the Wilson Research Group studies, the published mean share of project time spent in verification stayed between 53% and 57% from 2010 to 2020, while first-silicon success fell from about 32% in 2020 to 24% in 2022. Although the 2024 study reported 14% [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024], recruitment changed that year from industry lists to a qualified sample provider, and this methodological break, together with elevated nonresponse on some 2024 questions, prevents treating the two periods as equivalent measurements of the same population [@Foster2026SurveyMethodologyEvolution]. The reports establish substantial verification work and persistent respins, most often associated with logic or functional flaws, without establishing that added verification caused worse outcomes.

![**Verification surveys report substantial effort and persistent first-silicon failures.** Published verification time (2010–2020), first-silicon success (2014–2024), and staffing ratios (2007–2024); hollow staffing points are derived from growth rates [@Foster2013WilsonPart5; @Foster2015TrendsFunctionalVerification; @Foster2021WilsonPart8; @Foster2021WilsonPart12; @Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy; @Foster2023WilsonPart12; @Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. The 2024 recruitment change breaks direct comparability with 2007–2022 [@Foster2026SurveyMethodologyEvolution]. Lines connect available observations without establishing causality.](images/fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors){#fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors width="100%" fig-alt="Survey chart showing verification time shares of 53 to 57 percent through 2020 and first-silicon success of about 32 percent in 2020 and 24 percent in 2022. A shaded methodological break separates the 2024 result of 14 percent and its staffing ratio from the earlier series."}

The reported respin causes span logic, analog integration, clock-domain crossings, timing, and hardware–firmware behavior [@Foster2025WilsonVerification2024]. Clock-domain crossings, for example, require attention to metastability as well as the logical sequence seen by a testbench.[^fn-metastability-c02] More random stimulus alone may poorly exercise a rare interaction; directed tests, suitable constraints, assertions, and formal analysis can target what is missing. The useful question is which failure mechanisms the current checks can detect.

[^fn-metastability-c02]: **Metastability and clock-domain crossings (CDCs)**: A bistable storage element can enter a metastable state when an asynchronous input violates setup or hold timing constraints; its settling time has no guaranteed finite upper bound. Signals crossing asynchronous clock domains need a suitable crossing scheme, such as a multi-stage synchronizer for a single control signal or a handshake and asynchronous first-in, first-out queue for data transfers. These schemes reduce failure risk and preserve the intended communication, while ordinary cycle-accurate testbenches do not represent the intermediate analog voltages.

Escaped defects also differ in how they can be repaired, since some permit a firmware or software workaround that may sacrifice performance or functionality while others require revised silicon. Whereas Intel's \$475M charge associated with the Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) defect illustrates the potential cost of a shipped hardware error [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Intel1995PentiumCharge], Spectre and Meltdown illustrate a different problem, in which microarchitectural behavior undermines software's security assumptions [@LippEtAl2018Meltdown; @KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. Together these cases motivate early detection without establishing one universal cost multiplier for every late defect.

A new candidate may need new verification work before its performance matters. Published RTL-generation benchmarks include failures at parsing, interface compliance, and functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM; @WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Those tests do not establish timing closure or system correctness, but they show why a plausible description is only a starting point. The cost and latency of producing and checking a candidate depend on its scope, the reused verification infrastructure, and the required assurance; there is no fixed generation-to-verification ratio across abstraction levels.

The same data bound what Layer 1 point assistance can be expected to deliver on its own. Although a generator that drafts an isolated leaf module or testbench inside a human-specified pipeline speeds up one part of implementation, the surveys place much of the effort elsewhere: verification staffing grew at more than twice the annual rate of design staffing (@fig-verification-demand-scissors), and verification occupied more than half of reported project time in the 2010 to 2020 studies (@fig-ch07-wilson-verification-scissors), while the cost estimate discussed in @sec-design-cost-pressure assigns most of a leading-node budget to software, verification, and IP qualification. Faster drafting therefore helps only if the drafted modules do not add more integration and checking work than they save, such as reconnecting mismatched ports, resolving clock-domain crossings, clearing lint violations, and debugging corner-case deadlocks, which is a measurement a team must make rather than a conclusion to assume in either direction.

Generating the tests does not escape this bottleneck by itself. When one generator writes both a design and its testbench from the same specification, a shared misreading of an edge case can appear in both: the tests pass while the design is wrong, reproducing the correlated-failure problem that @sec-moonshot introduced through the Knight–Leveson experiment [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. The check therefore needs a reference the generator cannot edit, such as assertions derived from the architectural contract or a golden reference model, as @sec-feedback-verification-trust develops.

Verification effort belongs in the architectural comparison when alternatives differ in the tests, properties, and integration work they require. Reusing a familiar interface may preserve much of that investment; changing the organization may require new checks. The resulting engineering cost, together with implementation and software work, determines which promising designs a program can afford to develop.

\FloatBarrier

## The Economics of Specialized Silicon {#sec-design-cost-pressure}

```{=latex}
\suppressfloats[t]
```

The implementation and verification work described above consumes a finite development budget. Much of that work is non-recurring engineering (NRE): an investment in the design, software, and qualification that precedes production. Its scale matters both when choosing an architecture and when deciding how many alternatives to develop in detail.

Public estimates illustrate the size of this investment (@fig-design-cost-by-node), with the most widely quoted series coming from International Business Strategies (IBS). A 2018 IBS series put IC design cost at \$51.3M for a 28\ nm planar device, \$297.8M at 7\ nm, and \$542.2M at 5\ nm [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm], while the Semiconductor Industry Association quotes the same order of magnitude, more than \$540M for a 5\ nm design in 2020 [@SemiconductorIndustryAssociation2026ChipDesign], and Arm's 2023 prospectus, citing a July 2022 IBS estimate, gives \$249M at 7\ nm and \$725M at 2\ nm [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. Because the two vintages disagree at 7\ nm, each estimate rests on its own assumptions about die size, IP reuse, and what counts as design cost; although project budgets vary widely around any of these figures, both series show development cost rising steeply toward the leading edge.

```{python}
#| label: fig-design-cost-by-node
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Leading-node design-cost estimates rise steeply, and they depend on the estimate's vintage.** Each bar is an
#|   International Business Strategies (IBS) estimate, labeled with the year of the IBS series it comes from
#|   [@LaPedus2018BigTrouble3nm; @ArmHoldings2023Prospectus]. The two vintages differ at 7\ nm (\$298M versus \$249M),
#|   so the bars are published estimates under different assumptions, not a controlled node-scaling series or universal project prices.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bar chart of IC design-cost estimates by process node. The 2018 estimates are 51 million dollars at 28 nanometers, 298 million at 7 nanometers, and 542 million at 5 nanometers. The 2022 estimates, drawn hatched, are 249 million at 7 nanometers and 725 million at 2 nanometers."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv (rows with plotted == yes).
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(_root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-leading-node-design-cost.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")) if r["plotted"] == "yes"]
# Largest node first; within a node, older vintage first.
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-float(r["node_nm"]), r["estimate_vintage"]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
positions = list(range(len(rows)))
for pos, r in zip(positions, rows):
    cost = float(r["cost_musd"])
    newer = r["estimate_vintage"].endswith("2022")
    ax.barh(pos, cost, height=0.58, color=COLORS["constraints_tint"], edgecolor=COLORS["constraints"],
            linewidth=1.4, hatch="////" if newer else None, zorder=3)
    ax.text(cost + 12, pos, f"${cost:,.0f}M", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7,
            fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"], zorder=4)
    ax.text(cost + 100, pos, r["estimate_vintage"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6,
            color=COLORS["muted"], zorder=4)

ax.set_yticks(positions)
ax.set_yticklabels([f"{float(r['node_nm']):g} nm" for r in rows], fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 1000)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated IC design cost (US$M)", fontsize=7, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.5)
ax.grid(True, axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The composition of a design budget helps identify where assistance could matter. In the IBS 2\ nm estimate cited by Arm, software development, verification, and IP qualification together account for 71% of the total [@ArmHoldings2023Prospectus], and although this is a cost allocation for that estimate rather than the fraction of every project's critical path, it shows why faster RTL drafting alone cannot be assumed to remove most development expense.

The same allocation suggests a hypothesis about where each operational layer could reduce cost, which only measurements of real programs can test. The prospectus does not identify RTL drafting's share of the remaining 29%, so that remainder cannot be read as the cost of drafting or physical design alone. Point assistance (Layer 1) that drafts leaf RTL acts on part of that remainder, so its effect on total NRE depends on whether the drafted code adds more review, integration, and verification work than it saves. Parameter search inside a qualified container (Layer 2) can preserve existing interface verification and qualified IP, which limits its verification cost but also limits the design changes it can reach. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would target the 71% share only if it could generate verification collateral, compiler support, and qualification evidence that reviewers accept at lower total cost than conventional practice; the public end-to-end demonstration examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect does not report that comparison.

Production volume determines how that upfront investment contributes to each shipped unit. A simple accounting model makes the relationship explicit:

$$
C_{\mathrm{unit}} = C_{\mathrm{variable}} + \frac{C_{\mathrm{NRE}}}{V},
$$

where $C_{\mathrm{variable}}$ is the average manufacturing, packaging, and test cost per shipped unit, $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ is the allocated development investment, and $V$ is shipment volume. Within the variable term, die area $A$ and defect density $D_0$ govern silicon cost per good die (approximated in the Poisson model by $Y=e^{-A D_0}$, though defect clustering and other manufacturing effects require more detailed yield models). Because smaller dies reduce the silicon discarded when pre-assembly testing detects a defect, chiplet disaggregation can lower die cost, even as assembly yield, die-to-die interfaces, and advanced packaging take back part of that gain depending on the product's process and packaging parameters. Although this accounting model omits financing, pricing, and time-to-market effects, it exposes the central trade-off: a specialized design that saves enough energy or system cost to justify its development must carry a larger share of $C_{\mathrm{NRE}}$ per unit at lower volume, unless the team expands effective volume by reusing a modular chiplet across multiple products.

For a mobile-XR program, the architectural question is whether the expected efficiency and functionality justify the custom hardware, software, and checking work at its anticipated volume. Reusing IP, retaining programmable execution for changing workloads, or choosing a less aggressive process may improve that balance. Each choice can also affect power, performance, and schedule. The useful comparison includes those consequences rather than assuming either that custom silicon is unaffordable or that specialization always pays.

An evaluation budget is part of the same calculation. Spending more on a simulation or integration test can be worthwhile if it resolves an uncertainty that would otherwise cause expensive redesign. Generating more candidates can also be worthwhile if they offer meaningful alternatives. Their value depends on what the complete study learns for the resources it consumes, which brings the chapter's separate pressures back together.

## Compounding Loop Pressures {#sec-compounding-design-loop-pressure}

The preceding sections examined distinct costs, but a design study encounters them together. A different memory organization may need new compiler support; that software changes traffic, which affects the physical and system comparison. Some candidates can reuse existing checks, while others require new verification work. The effort needed to learn from one alternative therefore depends on more than the cost of proposing it.

This tight coupling matters because optimizing one stage often shifts the bottleneck elsewhere. Generating candidates faster, for example, can simply lengthen the simulation queue. Design-space size and evaluation capacity are different quantities, and enlarging the first does nothing for the second.

Rather than hunting for a single universal bottleneck, engineering teams should identify the specific work that throttles progress. Teams can measure the age and size of simulation or verification queues, track the fraction of candidates rejected as illegal, or count repeated tool runs and changing inputs. Reviewers can also monitor where results stall waiting for expert judgment. Industry trends supply context, but only measurements from the program itself can show what is constraining it.

The MAESTRO anchor in @tbl-design-loop-scale-anchors helps make that diagnosis concrete. Because its reported analytical throughput makes a large space affordable to score, a program using such a model should examine work on either side of the search before paying for a faster optimizer. Whereas upstream rankings depend on the workload description, since changed layer shapes or batch sizes could make an otherwise accurate analytical comparison irrelevant to deployment, downstream recommendations about implementation may require checks the analytical tier cannot supply, exposing two distinct bottlenecks around the model.

This diagnosis includes wasted work as well as slow work. A simulator run against the wrong workload occupies a slot without resolving the pending question, even if it completes successfully. Correcting the inputs can improve useful throughput without making the simulator itself faster.

This possibility extends the classic *design productivity gap*, documented in the 1999 ITRS, restated in its 2001 edition [@ITRS2001Design], and reiterated in the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and Semiconductor Industry Association Decadal Plan [@SRCSIA2021DecadalPlan]. Earlier abstraction shifts made larger designs tractable through RTL synthesis and IP reuse. Where candidate construction becomes cheaper, the corresponding challenge is whether simulation, verification, and review can absorb the additional work.

Not every constraint appears as a queue. A study may be waiting for a missing trace or supplier constraint, or its available organizations may all fail the target. In the latter case, faster evaluation of the same alternatives will not produce a feasible design. The architect may need to reconsider the organization, or the requirements, before scheduling more runs.

A backlog grows when a program admits more evaluation and review work than it completes over the same interval (@fig-scissors-gap). Generation supplies proposals; admission determines which ones enter the checking loop. Candidate counts alone can obscure the imbalance because alternatives differ in simulation time, physical checks, and required reviewer effort. Teams therefore need to compare arrivals and completions within each checking stage, along with the work each candidate requires. Admitting fewer candidates, screening them before expensive checks, or increasing the limiting stage's capacity can rebalance the loop.

The operational layers affect that backlog through the work they admit and the choices they can change. While Layer 1 assistance that lowers the cost of drafting candidates can grow the backlog if the team submits more work without increasing checking capacity, Layer 2 optimization can automate selection within a fixed container, using fast surrogates or direct physical checks as the study requires, and an AI-native design system (Layer 3) may also change the interfaces and organization under study, potentially requiring new checks. Because all three must preserve the assurance needed for the result, whether an intervention shrinks the backlog depends on admission policy, checking capacity, and how often surviving proposals fail later review, making that outcome a claim to measure rather than a property the layer confers.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size workflow needs flexible placement beside the conditional backlog discussion. -->
![**Backlog depends on admitted work and completed checks.** This unscaled flow diagram separates proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review. Waiting work grows at a stage when admissions exceed completions over the same interval; candidate counts must be interpreted alongside the different checking costs they impose. Admission and staged screening control how much generated work reaches the limited resources. The diagram specifies no measured rates or trend with architectural scope.](images/fig-scissors-gap){#fig-scissors-gap width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Unscaled flow diagram connecting proposal generation, admission, evaluation, and review to a completed decision. Waiting work is distinguished from completed checks; admission and screening determine which proposals enter the checking loop."}

Queue ages, admitted work, and completed checks turn this diagram into a diagnosis for a particular program. Cheaper generation can encourage the team to admit more work, but that response is a choice about how to spend the saved effort. A familiar observation from resource economics helps explain why total demand need not fall when one activity becomes cheaper.

::: {.callout-law title="The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation"}
**The principle.** Greater efficiency can encourage increased consumption that outstrips the initial savings, a rebound effect Jevons documented for coal consumption [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion]. In automated chip design, cheaper proposal generation can increase total resource consumption if the team responds by admitting enough additional evaluation and review work, even when downstream capacity stays fixed.

**The design implication.** If cheaper RTL generation leads a team to submit more candidates to simulation and implementation checks, demand for compute and EDA licenses can rise. The generation saving remains real; the complete study may nevertheless consume more resources.

**The response.** Choose how many candidates to admit and which evaluations each needs, then measure total effort and useful results. Admission limits and staged screening are possible controls (@sec-law-jevons-paradox in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Targeting AI Assistance {#sec-where-ai-assistance-targets-design-pressures}

The diagnosis becomes useful when it changes where the team spends its assistance budget. If a missing executable artifact prevents evaluation from starting, drafting that artifact may advance the study. If hundreds of candidates already await simulation, another generator may add delay, while screening or tool automation may help. The same method can therefore be useful in one program and poorly targeted in another.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Relieve the true limiting constraint"}
**The principle.** Target optimization directly at the bottleneck that actively delays the design decision. Common limiting factors include stale architectural models, long physical simulation runtimes, unpruned candidate sets, and the time senior engineers spend triaging failures.

**The application.** Assess whether assistance reduces the total effort or delay needed to answer the question. Include preparation and review costs, and preserve the checks that the decision requires. The limiting work may change as the study progresses.
:::

These needs suggest several possible uses of AI, from retrieving design information and screening candidates to drafting testbenches and guiding search. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops the method choices. Here the purpose is to connect a possible intervention to the work it could save.

For changing software, an automated regression pipeline can rerun the same benchmark with a new compiler and flag a change in candidate rankings. Assistance might help explain which transformation caused the change or identify an input mismatch. The comparison still needs to distinguish an implementation improvement from a changed task. Some of this work may be served well by conventional automation, without a learned model.

The rows in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound pair possible assistance with the engineering work it might reduce and the checks that remain. Keeping them together stops a team from mistaking a faster local task for a completed architectural comparison.

| **Limiting work** | **How AI might help** | **Engineering work it could reduce** | **What still establishes the result** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Context is scattered or stale | Reconcile workload, interface, tool, and result information; flag missing details or stale assumptions. | Manual search across reports, repositories, traces, and prior studies. | Source provenance, versioning, coverage, and architectural judgment that the information is sufficient. |
| Strong evaluation is scarce | Estimate performance, power, physical risk, or uncertainty before a stronger tool is run. | High-fidelity evaluations spent on candidates unlikely to change design decisions. | Calibration against stronger tools, coverage of the relevant design region, and checks on finalists. |
| A needed artifact is missing | Draft RTL, compiler code, tests, constraints, or candidate organizations. | Repetitive artifact creation and the initial pass through a design choice. | Interface rules, compilation or synthesis, verification, and physical checks appropriate to the artifact. |
| The choice space exceeds the budget | Search mappings, schedules, parameters, or topologies under stated objectives and constraints. | Manual sweeps and repeated selection among large numbers of choices. | A complete objective, legal choices, matched evaluation budgets, and stronger evaluation of the selected result. |
| Tool operation or triage consumes attention | Configure tools, launch runs, classify failures, compare reports, and route uncertain cases. | Repeated tool operation and initial result triage. | Clean tool state, reproducible commands, declared tool results, and expert review where required. |
: **Match assistance to the limiting work and retain the necessary checks.** Each row identifies a possible saving and the evidence needed to use its output in a design decision. {#tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound tbl-colwidths="[22,28,24,26]"}

These roles do not determine the workflow by themselves; the three operational layers organize them by how much of the design the automated work may change. Applied to the limits in @tbl-ai-contributions-by-bound, point assistance (Layer 1) fits rows where one artifact is missing and the surrounding design is settled; its result still passes through the integration and verification work described above. Search inside a fixed container (Layer 2) fits rows where the choice space exceeds the budget but the interfaces are right. It reaches its limit when no permitted change can relieve the bottleneck, as when neither reuse nor batching can compensate for a fixed offload path. An AI-native design system (Layer 3) would be a candidate response when the existing formulation itself excludes useful organizations. Its broader exploration still requires checks appropriate to the result, including static timing, design rules, formal properties, and power integrity where relevant. Prediction, generation, and optimization can contribute to all three; the distinction is how the design work is organized and which choices it can revisit.

The cost of assistance also belongs in the comparison. A surrogate may require data from expensive evaluations; generated candidates require checking; and tool-using systems consume compute, licenses, and review time. These investments may be worthwhile, but leaving them out can make displaced work look like a saving.

Rejecting AI assistance entirely is a legitimate outcome of the evaluation whenever an established deterministic method already solves the limiting task within budget. A learned method has a poor case when representative training data are unavailable, an adequate independent check cannot be constructed, or training, inference, tool calls, and added review cost more than the engineering work saved. Where analytical evaluation is already cheap, replacing it with a learned surrogate may save little, whereas a screening predictor calibrated against expensive cycle simulation or physical checks may be worth costing regardless of the raw candidate count; if the primary obstacle is an infeasible requirement, the appropriate response is to reformulate the architecture question or decline further search.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="No single method carries the Lighthouse moonshot"}
**Context.** Lighthouse begins with an XRBench-class mobile workload, a 64-bit RISC-V basis, a 3\ W target, and a 3\ nm-class process. It leaves workload instances, memory organization, compiler support, and implementation choices to be developed into a study. The earlier cache and offload examples show why those choices must be considered together across the operational layers.

**Application.** A Layer 1 approach might ask a generator to draft an isolated vector arithmetic leaf cell or scratchpad controller, leaving engineers to connect buses, resolve clock-domain crossings, and debug races. A Layer 2 approach might fix the 64-bit pipeline and sweep cache capacities and unroll factors against a cycle simulator. It would reach its limit if no permitted configuration could keep memory traffic within the 3\ W budget or relieve routing congestion; expanding the search would then require revisiting the container's boundaries.

A Layer 3 AI-native design system, if one could be built for this problem, would be permitted to set the processor template aside and propose a streaming tensor datapath, custom arithmetic, tiled scratchpad memories, and matched compiler loop schedules from the XRBench intent and formal signoff assertions. Testing those candidates against the 3\ W target requires workload-dependent power analysis with a defined measurement boundary and averaging interval, whereas checking thermal feasibility requires the package's heat-removal conditions and static timing and dynamic IR-drop analyses address separate timing and power-delivery obligations. Because the public end-to-end demonstration examined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect addresses a smaller processor problem, it leaves open whether this XRBench prompt can be carried through to a checked result.

**Outcome.** An AI-native design system earns adoption only when its candidates satisfy the verified silicon constraints and, against a credible conventional alternative, it improves the result, reduces the total engineering cost of reaching a comparable result, or both, rather than merely chaining a generator to an EDA tool or producing a novel design description.
:::

The resulting test is practical: did the chosen assistance help the team answer its architecture question, with the required checks and an honest account of the work? A useful local tool can pass that test without carrying the complete Lighthouse workflow. A broader design system must demonstrate the additional capability its coordination is intended to provide. The architect remains responsible for interpreting the comparison and deciding what further work or review the result warrants.

\FloatBarrier

## Open Questions

The pressures traced in this chapter show why architectural progress can stall on data movement, offload overhead, physical signoff, or verification capacity rather than raw candidate generation. Turning that diagnosis into rigorous automation exposes five open research problems across computer architecture, electronic design automation, and machine learning:

- **How should an exploration harness throttle candidate admission when cheap generation saturates downstream simulation and verification queues?** Lowering the cost of drafting register-transfer level (RTL) modules or compiler schedules can trigger a Jevons rebound, flooding cycle-accurate simulators, place-and-route licenses, and human reviewers with more candidates than downstream stages can clear. Because candidates vary widely in simulation runtime, physical routability, and verification surface, static batch sizes either starve scarce tools or accumulate multi-day backlogs. Formulating admission control policies that price expected downstream verification effort against expected information gain remains an open problem across computer architecture and EDA.

- **How can fast screening proxies detect physical waterbed inversions when search leaves a characterized accelerator template?** Analytical models and learned surrogates can score millions of loop mappings or datapath configurations per hour, but they remain calibrated to the interconnect topologies, static random-access memory (SRAM) banking rules, and switching profiles of existing templates. When a generator proposes an unfamiliar topology, reductions in local arithmetic energy can trigger unmodeled off-chip memory traffic, routing congestion, or inductive $L\frac{di}{dt}$ voltage droops that invert candidate rankings at physical signoff. Determining which low-cost physical invariants or uncertainty estimates can flag these proxy inversions before committing full place-and-route runs is a central problem for multi-fidelity search.

- **Can architectural search price verification complexity alongside power, performance, and area before RTL is written?** A speculative cache-coherence optimization or decoupled asynchronous interface may improve simulated throughput while multiplying reachable transient states, clock-domain crossings, and formal proof obligations beyond the program's verification budget. Existing exploration frameworks treat power, performance, and area (PPA) as the primary objective and treat verification as a fixed downstream tax, even though verification accounts for the majority of leading-node development effort. Defining structural complexity metrics that predict bounded model checking depth, simulation coverage convergence, and assertion reuse would let optimizers penalize designs that are fast in simulation but intractable to verify.

- **How can architects quantify the option value of hardware flexibility when workloads and numerical formats shift faster than silicon schedules?** Hardwiring a fixed dataflow, scratchpad capacity, or block-scale number format maximizes peak throughput per watt on current benchmarks, but risks falling below the LogCA break-even granularity $g^*$ or operational-intensity threshold $\mathrm{OI}^*$ when deployment shifts toward sparse mixture-of-experts routing or paged key-value caches. Retaining programmable vector engines, reconfigurable interconnect fabrics, or spare on-chip memory preserves adaptability across a multi-year silicon lifecycle at an immediate price in die area and static leakage. Formulating stochastic co-design objectives that weigh present efficiency against modeled distributions of future kernel shapes and compiler schedules remains an open challenge.

- **How can automated exploration synthesize safe composition contracts across encrypted IP blocks and multi-vendor chiplets?** System-on-chip (SoC) and chiplet architects routinely integrate third-party processors, memory controllers, and Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) die-to-die links supplied as fixed hard macros or encrypted RTL whose internal queuing, power-state transitions, and clock-domain crossings cannot be inspected. While transaction-level standards specify pin handshakes, undocumented buffer occupancy limits or thermal coupling across die boundaries can still cause system-level deadlocks or tail-latency violations under bursty traffic. Developing active probing strategies and gray-box interface contracts that bound compositional latency, power delivery, and protocol liveness without exposing proprietary netlists would open multi-vendor systems to automated exploration.

## Summary

Architectural gains increasingly depend on how microarchitecture, specialization, software, and physical implementation work together. The examples in this chapter make the consequences concrete: a faster arithmetic block can lose to offload overhead, a wider vector grouping can increase spills, and lower compute energy can be outweighed by memory traffic. A useful comparison includes the interactions capable of changing its outcome.

Investigating those alternatives consumes implementation effort, evaluation capacity, and verification work. A large search space does not by itself establish an expensive study, and an expensive study does not by itself establish a need for AI. The opportunity depends on the work that limits progress, the alternatives assistance could make practical, and the total cost of obtaining results that answer the architecture question. An AI-native design system is one possible response when the existing formulation excludes useful organizations; its value remains something to demonstrate.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Follow the costs of a local improvement.** Include data movement, control, software overhead, and physical effects before treating a block-level gain as a system gain.
- **Evaluate hardware with its software.** Compiler mappings, runtime behavior, and workload changes can alter which organization is useful.
- **Choose the boundary that answers the question.** Model the interactions that can change the decision, using appropriate abstractions for each scale.
- **Budget for learning from candidates.** Candidate counts, simulation throughput, verification effort, and development cost describe different constraints. Tests, models, and proofs also establish different things.
- **Target assistance and measure the complete result.** Use the workflow and methods the problem needs, including conventional automation. Count preparation, evaluation, and review as well as the task that became faster.
:::

Once a team identifies the work delaying its next decision, it needs a way to organize the study around it. A simulator result must remain tied to the workload and candidate it evaluated, and a failed check must guide the next design action. @sec-architecture-20-ontology develops that organization through six stages: Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit. Together they connect the architecture question to candidate development, evaluation, interpretation, and the decision about what to do next.
